subsubtopic: INTEREST RATE-AMENDMENT TO ASSIST SMALL BORROWERS-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, i rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43.
In light of the fact that the Small Loans Act requires any lending institution which charges in excess of 12 per cent per year to be licensed by the federal government, and in light of the fact that such a regulation no longer makes it financially profitable for credit unions to lend small amounts of money, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson):
That the minister in charge of consumer and corporate affairs be required to introduce a bill before the end of the current session to amend the Small Loans Act so that the mandatory 1 2 per cent ceiling is no longer effective, thus making it possible for credit unions and other similar lending establishments to serve the people that they were primarily intended to serve-the small borrowers.

subsubtopic: LAY-OFFS IN P E L-REQUEST CNR REVERSE DECISION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. This week Canadian National Railways has laid off one-half of its rail car repairmen on Prince Edward Island, with only 14 days' notice to the men involved, despite the fact that most of these men have given over 30 years of dedicated service to their employer. Four of them have given 140 years combined service. Given that those lay-offs constitute a most serious further downgrading of the
railway on Prince Edward Island, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. Gass):
That this House condemn Canadian National Railways for its heartless treatment of rail car repairmen on Prince Edward Island; and, further, that this House urge CN to reverse its lay-off decision so that P.E.I. rail cars can continue to be maintained and repaired on Prince Edward Island rather than in another jurisdiction.

CANCER-CAUSING DRUGS IN CURED MEATS-CALL FOR BAN-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to move a motion under Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.

May 30, 1980
In view of the fact that a recent study done by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology confirmed that nitrates and nitrites when consumed can cause cancer, and in view of the fact that these drugs are still being used extensively in Canada in processing cured meats such as bacon, ham, weiners, etc., which when consumed form nitrosomines, a well-known cancer-causing agent, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie):
That the Department of National Health and Welfare take immediate steps to completely ban the use of nitrites and nitrates in food curing and processing, which will speed up the development of alternative methods of curing meat not harmful to the human body.

subsubtopic: REQUEST INTEREST RATE REVIEWED PERIODICALLY-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I hope my motion under Standing Order 43 will secure the required unanimous consent of this House, because it deals with a matter of immediate, pressing and national concern and importance.
Because Canadian government annuities have been bearing interest at only 7 per cent since 1975, when a promise was made to review that interest rate, and with the interest rate now standing at over 11 per cent, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain):
That this House require the government to live up to the undertaking given in February, 1976, by the then minister responsible for the annuity program, Mr. Robert Andras, to the effect that "both the increase in the rate of interest and the percentage increase in the annuity (at maturity) will be subject to periodic review" and, in addition, that the government be required to take appropriate steps so that adjustments may be made from time to time to keep the interest rate on government annuities more closely aligned to interest rates in the marketplace.

subtopic: REFINERIES TO UPGRADE HEAVY OILS-GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE
REFINERIES TO UPGRADE HEAVY OILS-GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. He will recall that on May 15, in a speech, he indicated government involvement to fulfil the very obvious need for refineries in Ontario and in Quebec to instal facilities to assist in heavy oil upgrading to maximize, of course, the productivity of the crude oil they process. One of the refineries he mentioned specifically in that speech was the Ultramar Golden Eagle refinery at Quebec City. I wonder if the minister could advise the House today if this upgrading at this particular refinery includes government assistance such as grants, loans and tax benefits.
Specifically, because he indicated in the speech greater access by that refinery to Canadian crude, can the minister confirm that he proposes to allocate Ultramar an additional 50,000 barrels a day, or some such approximate amount, of Canadian crude which would be diverted from the Montreal area refineries, which refineries receive this crude through the Sarnia-Montreal pipeline?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: REFINERIES TO UPGRADE HEAVY OILS-GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, there is no intention to provide for grants or subsidies for this particular conversion at the Ultramar refinery. However, in order to achieve the purpose we are trying to achieve, of upgrading the treatment of oil at that particular refinery, we are working on an arrangement whereby greater access to Canadian domestic oil will be provided to the Ultramar refinery. Obviously, this will imply reallocation between the various other refineries at the present time. That is in the works and I expect that it will be worked out very shortly.

subtopic: REFINERIES TO UPGRADE HEAVY OILS-GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, when the minister refers to "other refineries", my information was that it was the Montreal area. The minister may wish to confirm that. What concerns me-and the minister will recall, because many of his colleagues raised it last year-is that it was Ultramar which cut off so many Quebec and Ontario independents. There was one in my own riding as well, so it was not a problem unique to Quebec.
However, would such diversion not be against the advice of department officials, who were informed of numerous accusations made against Ultramar to the effect that Ultramar shorted its Quebec City refinery by selling about 50,000 barrels a day on the spot market in order to secure higher profits? There are those accusations on the one hand, and on the other hand there is the vulnerability of the small Canadian independents in both Quebec and Ontario who rely very heavily on that refinery and were cut off arbitrarily.
Oral Questions
That company does not enjoy the best reputation in the industry, and 1 am wondering what we are doing to ensure that the situation will be improved by that particular refinery

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: REFINERIES TO UPGRADE HEAVY OILS-GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE
speechtext: I am indeed quite pleased to see that my colleague is raising that very important question and I can assure him that it is one to which we attach much importance. I already had the opportunity to meet with the independent dealers of Ontario and Quebec and we discussed the matter. 1 also had the opportunity to meet with some representatives of Ultramar and to point out our dissatisfaction about the situation in recent years. The developments to which we are now referring should boost the production of that refinery and make it available to independent dealers. We intend to follow the matter closely and see that independent dealers are truly protected so that there will be no discrimination against them compared with the dealers related to the multinationals. The Ultramar project should increase the heating oil and gas available while the Petro-Canada project to build a large upgrading refinery in eastern Montreal should also encourage in the years to come an increase in gas and other petroleum products available to the independents. We keep this question constantly in mind while we are working out the developments that have been announced.

I have a final supplementary question, Madam Speaker. I hope the minister will go beyond expressing dissatisfaction, because he is in a very excellent bargaining position. In that regard, my final supplementary deals with the government's pledge to Canadianize the industry.
As the minister knows, Ultramar is 100 per cent foreign owned. He indicated in a speech that he had secured certain undertakings from Ultramar, although not respecting Canadian ownership. Given the minister's excellent bargaining position, given the pledge with respect to the Canadianization program, what undertakings, if any, is he seeking from Ultramar with respect to the Canadianization of its Canadian subsidiary?

subtopic: REFINERIES TO UPGRADE HEAVY OILS-GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE

The government is at present working on such a broad approach. In a speech on May 15 in Montreal, the minister indicated he had an understanding from Ultramar to complete this upgrading facility on condition that the federal government would direct to it Canadian crews from other Montreal refiners.
However, as the minister should be aware, under the 1979 agreement with FIRA, related to Ultramar's purchase of Canadian Fuel Marketers, Ultramar is required to build an upgrading facility. My question to the minister is very simple: why is he now bribing Ultramar to do what it is already required to do under the FIRA agreement?

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is certainly not a question of bribing anybody, and Ultramar in particular. It is a question of reducing our dependence on imported oil, increasing the higher processing, the upgrading of oil through our refineries in Canada. This is going to be achieved, and the net result will mean, I hope, reducing our dependence on foreign oil.
I think this is a very welcome development in terms of the refineries in Sarnia, in terms of the refineries in eastern Montreal and what Ultramar will do at the present time.

Madam Speaker, the minister has not answered the question as to why he is penalizing the Montreal refiners to benefit this Quebec City refiner; why he is allocating profit among companies.
As the minister is aware, refineries in Atlantic Canada are suffering just as serious a problem with excessive residuals. Indeed, the Gulf refinery in Point Tupper will be shut down for three months, laying off workers in Cape Breton, as a result of the same problem.

Oral Questions ENERGY

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. On May 13, the B.C. energy minister said that the federal minister of energy would not give an assurance that an export tax on natural gas would not be imposed on British Columbia gas exports.
During the election campaign, on February 13 Mr. Gordon Gibson, a three-time federal Liberal candidate, former Liberal MLA, past member of the Prime Minister's staff and past leader of the Liberal party in B.C., said:

subsubtopic: DENIAL OF COUNSEL TO DEFEND MEMBER OF RCMP
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Solicitor General. As the minister knows, Sergeant A1 Godin, a 20-year veteran of the RCMP and a member of the security service, has been charged under the code of offences in the RCMP Act with respect to certain allegations of smoking marijuana, based on the allegations of another member of the force. He requested the right to counsel at his trial, and has been denied that by the force.
Will the minister assure the House that minimum standards of justice, such as the right to retain counsel, will be accorded to Sergeant Godin in circumstances where his reputation, his livelihood and his future are in peril?

subsubtopic: DENIAL OF COUNSEL TO DEFEND MEMBER OF RCMP
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as I understand the situation, we are not dealing with a trial but with an internal discipline proceeding of the RCMP. I agree with the hon. member that the present procedure is unfair. I want to point out that its unfairness was noted by the Marin commission in 1976, when it made recommendations for change.
These recommendations are the subject of legislation which is under consideration by the government and which was referred to in the throne speech. It is a high priority of the government that it should be brought forward. When it is brought forward, I hope it will receive rapid consideration and approval by this House, so that the RCMP will have at least as fair a system, if not more fair, than that which applies to other police forces in Canada.

subsubtopic: DENIAL OF COUNSEL TO DEFEND MEMBER OF RCMP
speechtext: A supplementary question. Will the hon. minister agree with me that under the code of offences in the RCMP Act there is nothing to prohibit him from having the right to counsel now? Will he recommend to the commissioner of the RCMP that this man, whose livelihood and future are in jeopardy, be able to retain counsel to dispute the allegations made against him? Will the minister make that recommendation?

speechtext:

The Prime Minister has consistently refused to make clear his intentions on native people and the constitution, and he has directly refused the participation of elected members of the Yukon and Northwest Territorial governments in constitutional discussions.
I would like to ask the Prime Minister to clarify what his real intentions are regarding natives and the constitution, and to ask him to reverse his decision of yesterday which denies elected representatives of northern peoples' participation in the June 9 talks, so that northern Canadians are accorded the

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: PARTICIPATION OF NATIVE PEOPLE AND NORTHERNERS IN CONSTITUTIONAL DISCUSSIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, with regard to the role to be played by the native peoples and their leaders, 1 made a lengthy statement about three weeks ago at a meeting with those leaders and 1 would be happy to send a copy of it to the hon. member. I summed up the essence of it yesterday when 1 said they would be involved in discussions on any aspect of the constitution which directly affected them.
In so far as the Yukon and the Territories are concerned, Madam Speaker, 1 have not invented or created their status. They do not have the status of provinces. Under the constitution and under the constitutional conventions, the participation of the Territories is not needed for constitutional change, much as their advice has been, and will be, sought. That may be different if in days to come they achieve the status of provinces. But for the time being I repeat that the constitution and constitutional conventions do not provide room for the Territories as such to be negotiators on constitutional change, no more than they provide room, for instance, for the elected representatives of municipal governments who are legitimately representing the interests of the municipalities in which they are elected. They have no locus standi, in the legal sense, in constitutional discussions. That is the situation as the constitution states it, Madam Speaker.

speechtext:

May 30, 1980

Can the minister indicate what the involvement of the Department of Communications has been in this incident, and can he indicate whether it is the policy of the government to lay charges against Canadians living in remote areas of the country who have banded together to put up earth stations because they are unable to receive a variety of Canadian signals off air?

subsubtopic: LEGAL ACTION AGAINST OWNERS OF UNLICENSED EARTH STATIONS

Madam Speaker, I would like to inform the hon. member that there are two parts to the policy being pursued by the government in this respect. The first part is to try to reach the root of the problem and to have a variety of television programs available to residents of remote or nonmetropolitan communities in Canada.

We expect that the solution to the first part of the problem-extension of services to northern communities-will result from the present hearings of the CRTC on this very subject: we expect to have a report from the CRTC around June 15.

The CRTC and the Department of Communications are watching and following the situation closely. He said: Madam Speaker, may I say at the outset that I think drought is a most appropriate subject for debate on an opposition day on this Friday afternoon in Ottawa.
Before I get into the main content of my comments about drought, I want to make a brief remark and an obvious one about rain. 1 am referring, of course, to some good rains that began a week ago today in western Canada, mostly in Alberta. 1 would say very briefly that they were heaven sent and very, very welcome. They began last Friday afternoon and it seems that most of the heaviest rains followed along the foothills, along the western side of Alberta. The city of Lethbridge reported a three inch rain and Raymond, in the southwest corner of Alberta, was reported to have had five to six inches of rain, which is a very heavy rain. Incidentally, that rain lasted over a three to four day period.
In the southeast corner, my corner, Medicine Hat, we received a maximum of about one and a half inches. That was spread over about four days. I would say the heavy rains seemed to extend northward in Alberta and covered a good bit of the forest fire area in northern Alberta. Of course, that was a welcome change in the weather pattern. I would say it is not what we call a general rain, but over the weekend there was a series of showers which was very, very beneficial.
In Saskatchewan and Manitoba the situation is not nearly as good. The rainfall is considerably less, beginning right at the Alberta border and working east. Some areas, such as the Swift Current area, received hardly any rain. In Manitoba it is my understanding that the same situation exists, that is, very skimpy rainfalls over most of the province.
In spite of this very welcome rain-actually it is the first since early last fall-and in spite of the CBC's very glib
May 30, 1980

statement on the first day of the rain that the drought was over, 1 would say that the western drought definitely is not over. The considerable and substantial implications and aftermath of this drought are still with us. The western agricultural drought is certainly not over and that is what 1 want to talk about in the remainder of my remarks.
Let us examine this drought, its extent and the implications that flow from it. It begins in the interior of British Columbia and covers all of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. To the south it goes well into the United States, covering all of those border states along our western provinces, including what is known as the American northwest corn belt. Its northern extension in Canada is significantly further north than a drought has ever been known to extend before. 1 am thinking of the 1930s and the drought in 1977. In the north it extends right across the four western provinces as well. The extreme forest fire situation from British Columbia across Canada and well into northern Ontario is, of course, directly related to, and is an extension of, the southern prairie drought.
The current drought began early last fall across the west and it extended right through the winter. Yes, it is possible to have a winter drought; we had one last winter. The snowfall was exceedingly light, not only on the prairies but even across Ontario and into Quebec. In our short grass country, and that is usually the chinook belt, or all across southern Alberta and southwestern Saskatchewan, our snowfall was almost nil. The little snow moisture that resulted finally in the spring was completely lost by a month of not just warm but hot weather in April, with very strong, hot and dry winds.
Most of these drying winds, and I think this is unique and exceptional, came out of the east and southeast, a direction we usually associate with storms and moisture. It may or may not be significant, but this unusual wind and hot weather pattern did not change until Mount St. Helens blew its top and our traditional southwest Pacific winds returned, complete with the very depressing volcanic ash fallout.
The present drought situation, to date has been much more serious than the one-year drought of 1977 because it is so much broader in its coverage. The final assessment of this drought year will have to wait until the key month of June is over when rain in generous amounts must come to prevent a disaster in our agricultural growth year in the west.
Yesterday this subject of drought was raised in our first meeting of the Standing Committee on Agriculture, and today in this opposition debate is the first time this subject has come before this Parliament. I say very bluntly now that this drought debate should have taken place at least a month ago. The persistent questions in this House and in the Senate and the number of motions under Standing Order 43 certainly confirm that statement.
1 must say that I was very disappointed that my motion under Standing Order 26 for an emergency debate was denied about a week and a half ago.
Agricultural Drought
I repeat that our motion today is very appropriate, and I want to read it for emphasis. It is short and to the point and is as follows:
That this House deeply regrets the government's lack of response in the House of Commons to concern about the disastrous western agricultural drought and the related forest fire emergency, and calls on the government to abandon its secretive approach and consult with MPs of all parties in an open and forthright manner.
Surely this subject is much too important to be left to the traditional partisan, political type of debate. The subject is of widespread concern throughout western Canada, even after that good rain I said we have already received out there, and even in cities such as Calgary where the implications of a shortage of domestic water supplies are obvious. It is also a serious concern to our prairie governments, and because there has been no federal debate or action there is the perception- and I emphasize "perception"-in the west that this government and even this Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) do not care and do not know about the real drought situation in the west.
The subject of drought is at best distressing and unpleasant, but it should not be treated secretively, and especially we in Parliament should not be reluctant to talk about it. However, that situation does exist, mainly because politicians, of any stripe, cannot legislate or otherwise solve the climatic and geographic combinations which bring about droughts at irregular intervals. Suffice it to say that those of us from the short grass chinook country have learned how to pace ourselves or condition ourselves to live with a drought, and not to exist in spite of a drought, such as during those ten years in the 1930s and, more recently, the single drought years we had in 1961 and 1977.
I would say that it is almost a way of life. No one, however, can fully appreciate the true significance of a drought if he has not witnessed the tragedy of dust clouds hundreds of feet high rolling over the prairie like a black storm cloud-without moisture, of course-making it dark enough to require lights. That is a frightening experience. You cannot have a feel for drought if you have never witnessed, especially in the summer time, a large herd of cattle hungry because of no grass growth, or the spectacle of cattle becoming thirsty with no water immediately available. Hon. members should not hasten to tell me that these are management problems because these situations can develop, especially in the process of trailing large herds of cattle, even today. It is a frightening experience to see a herd of cattle on the trail suddenly and all at once stop walking and to see the cattle lift their heads into the wind when they can smell water upwind. It is almost an instant reaction. Have hon. members ever tried to smell water? Cattle can, but they cannot differentiate between fresh water and alkaline water, which is too concentrated to drink.
Western Canada has 45 million acres of grass suitable for grazing domestic livestock, and there are only 50,000 million acres of grass in that category in all of Canada. Our cattle industry and a relatively few sheep presently use nearly all of this grass. So drought has a special significance for our cattle, which harvest that grass year round. That is all they really do.

May 30, 1980
Agricultural Drought
They harvest our native grass mainly on a year round basis, and very often it is very short grass. During the 1930s we learned the hard way that during a drought you cut your cattle numbers to fit your supplies of grass and hay. You try to retain a bare minimum breeding herd to produce calves the next year. In a nutshell that is our objective in a drought.
Today, due to the extreme shortage of grass and hay, it is not practical to move cattle to another source of grass or hay or to move hay any distance to cattle. That applies all over western Canada where the drought is so severe. The reason is that there are simply no available supplies of grass or hay in western Canada either to move or to move to. It may be very significant before this drought is over that the only area with a surplus of both hay and grass at this moment is in the province of Ontario.
Southern Alberta's 950,000 acres of intensive irrigation will produce two good cuttings of alfalfa this year. It is a major irrigated crop in our intensive irrigation, but that crop will be competed for mainly by the dairy industries of the four western provinces from British Columbia right through and into Manitoba. Presently the last of the 1979 alfalfa crop in the Brooks area, which is the heart of one of the irrigation districts, is selling at as high as $100 a ton in the stack before being trucked to places like Red Deer, Alberta, and that is an area in central Alberta which has seldom been short of hay. It is a very unique situation.
That is the drought picture today as straightforward by and factually as I can describe it. And, of course, I should remind the House that these are my personal remarks.
What can we do about it here in our Thirty-second federal Parliament? I want to address myself to that for the remainder of my remarks. I have some suggestions for serious consideration by all of us.
I said that in the thirties we had to reduce our cattle numbers to fit our grass and hay supplies. That, of course, was long before the days of income tax. Today that lesson of the thirties is still valid, but it is complicated by our tax laws. Forced sales of feeder cattle and even breeding herds, up to as-much as one-half of some of our cattle herds-creates an impossible income tax situation.
The obvious answer is to recognize the merits of what is known as the deferred income averaging trust account which would allow cattlemen to build up their own tax protected stabilization fund, but on a personal basis. The Department of Finance is familiar with this well thought out proposal because it refused to consider it in the 1977 drought, when it was put to the department in a very serious suggestion at that time. The deferral should last long enough for cattle producers to rebuild their numbers by natural increase which will follow the drought period, or to buy back in, when grass and hay conditions return. That, of course, could take several years.
Another suggestion already widely recommended is to require the Canadian Wheat Board to guarantee sufficient supplies of barley in the west, and especially in Alberta, to feed out the increased number of feeder yearlings now going
into feedlots. These supplies must be assured now for use before the new crop is available. We should be aware that significantly increased numbers of drought cattle-and that includes some cow and calf pairs-have been coming to markets in the west over the last month.
We should consider the practical possibility of encouraging the earlier movement of feeder cattle to Ontario-that is, more so than the usual pattern-and even the possibility of a back haul of hay by both the railroads and by trucks. The cattle, of course, would remain in Ontario on grass as long as possible until the beginning of winter and then be moved into the Ontario feedlots to be finished out on corn and corn silage. Eventually they will go to the fat cattle market in Ontario, we hope at prices high enough to pay the $6 per hundredweight freight rate which it costs to move the cattle from the west to Ontario.
I suggest that surely here is a worthy possibility that will require financial assistance which should be forthcoming from two sources, not only from our federal government but from the railways in some form of special reduced rates, especially on the back haul with the hay, if that possibility should develop. I think it is a very practical suggestion. Years ago we used to have what the railways called a feeder rate for moving feeder cattle. That might be reinstated with some modification to help out in this situation.
Canada's beef cattle industry desperately needs some positive indication of confidence over the long-term. That has been apparent since we got into this market situation which we share with the hog industry across North America. What better way to do this than bring in our beef import or, if you like, meat import legislation now? It will get widespread support here in the House and, I am sure, from the total Canadian cattle industry.
I should now like to say something about PFRA, or the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Administration. It is the agency created out of the tragedy and despair of the dirty thirties. Its new director, Dr. Harry Hill, has initiated the beginning of a drought contingency program quite recently. Only a few of us in the House are aware of it, but it is certainly not a security item! I say most sincerely now: let us give solid support to this approach. After all, PFRA developed the original guidelines for the original drought, at least in modern times, which was in about the mid-thirties. Is it not about time that PFRA was returned home to agriculture here in the federal government?

What

That, perhaps, is the most serious thought I could leave with you. With all of our sophistication to date, whether in weather forecasting or in trying to modify the weather itself, there is no reason why there could not be another dirty thirties. Some of us on this side of the House have of necessity become unofficial experts on the subject of drought, whether we like it or not. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT RESPONSE REGARDING AGRICULTURAL DROUGHT AND FOREST FIRE EMERGENCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to have the opportunity to speak on the topic chosen by our friends in the Conservative party. However, I am saddened that the drought situation in the west is such that the topic is considered urgent enough to be the subject of today's debate.
1 was forcefully reminded of the seriousness of the situation in the west on the weekend when I heard the lowing of hungry cattle. It reminded me of the permanent drought area in the southern Sahara where I spent several years in the early 1970s as an educational adviser to the Kano state government in northern Nigeria. A million cattle starved in the drought conditions in the most appalling circumstances in a chronically food-short area. Hearing that sound again in my native Saskatchewan last weekend underlined how difficult the present circumstances are for livestock producers.
My colleague, the hon. member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse), who is our party's agriculture critic, is not here today because of the drought and the necessity for him to be on his farm to find accommodation for his cattle. As of yesterday when he was in contact with his office, only one tenth of one inch of rain had fallen in his area since last fall.
Although some of the areas in the west have had rain recently, there are large parts of Alberta, Manitoba and Saskatchewan that have had little or no rain. Each personal difficulty that a farmer is facing is multiplied thousands of times. We must as a country and a government be prepared to meet the challenges presented by this drought and the ones which will inevitably follow. To date we have had many words from the government opposite but precious little action.
Agricultural Drought
Here is the situation regarding cattle and cattle feed, as I see it. Pasture land is critical at this time of year and it is critical throughout most of the west. There is little excess feed for movement among the regions of the west. Farmers are therefore making do with what they have for pasture and in some cases letting their cattle graze on seeded acreage that is not yet at a stage where plants will be damaged; still others let their cattle graze on hay land. The best these farmers can hope for is to keep their cattle going until the middle or the end of June. If there is rain by that time-and how many times did we hear the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) in committee yesterday invoke the name of the Almighty in hoping for rain-some of the hay land may still produce one cut for feed next winter.
I say to the minister and hon. members opposite that the Almighty might not choose to bail us out this time. The minister might remember another phrase from another era when farmers were seeking action from reluctant governments. It was "raise less wheat and more hell". The minister can expect to hear more of that from this side of the House.
The drought crisis is taking place right now. Many farmers, particularly dairy farmers, are already having to feed cattle reserve stocks of feed. Herds are being trimmed right now. Producers will try to carry their core herds through until next fall, but not all will be able to manage on current stocks. Many herds were being cut in the past few months because of low prices and the projection of low prices into the future. Now, with more culling because of feed shortages, the cattle industry may nearly collapse. Can I ask the minister what will happen to the cattle industry now?
I cannot agree with the suggestion of the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) that the sale of breeding stock should be accelerated by the government's giving an income averaging annuity to producers.

speechtext:
Giving the farmer a tax dodge may help the big operator, but certainly it will not help the run-of-the-mill producers who are dependent on their breeding stocks confining from year to year, and the consumer will also pay considerably for the same beef when the herds have been diminished.
Surely the answer is a national meat authority which the minister has been asked repeatedly to establish. I understand he will be asked again by the ministers of agriculture in Toronto. Although he is not here, I call upon him to give a commitment to supply management in cattle just as he has given to other agricultural crops and animals in the past. Orderly marketing can give the Almighty and the minister a good deal of assistance. We need every bit of it.
The situation could improve if we could be sure of producing a substantial grain crop. However, there has been considerable damage to grain because of low germination rates, field pests such as grasshoppers, and the effects of hot, drying winds on available moisture and the crops. The government must be

May 30, 1980
Agricultural Drought
doing its forward planning with the probabilities in mind. First, there is not likely to be enough rain to rescue the present situation. Second, even if there is rain, hay and grain production will be minimal this year.
On this basis a drought contingency plan can be developed if the federal government would consider the matter seriously and put its money rather than its ministers' speeches and tours first. That has been this government's approach throughout the spring. It has been the political low road for various superannuated senators who have been playing at make-work projects such as Drought Inspector. It is a high paying make-work project. But let me illustrate how the travelling-circus on the political low road is upsetting my constituents and many ex-Liberal voters in the west.
Many members are aware that the deputy ministers of agriculture from the four western provinces met with the federal government two weeks ago and agreed to share costs in a drought relief program on a 50-50 basis, or at least that is what the provincial governments thought. They are dealing with drought on a day to day basis, and that is what they thought they had agreed to. But this week and yesterday in agriculture committee hearings the minister repudiated any agreement. He said such an arrangement required Treasury Board and cabinet approval. He scolded Saskatchewan agriculture minister Gordon MacMurchy for having the gall to say that a substantial drought relief program costing $15 million to $20 million had not been cost-shared with the province.

speechtext: There is no contradiction there.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT RESPONSE REGARDING AGRICULTURAL DROUGHT AND FOREST FIRE EMERGENCY
speechtext:
No one is saying that the Saskatchewan program will solve the drought crisis, but it may help those who are only partially able to cope. It is a rational approach to a desperate problem, yet the minister would only pour cold water, if he could find any, on a substantial effort by a provincial government. Unfortunately for the government, this ploy was uncovered. A cabinet document has been leaked which revealed the cynicism of the approach the federal government has been taking.
An interesting slice of this document appeared in a Canadian Press story in the Montreal Gazette on Wednesday. It reads as follows:
While it is recognized that because of the widespread nature of the drought and impact on the economy, responsive governmental programs will not have a large impact upon drought-related problems, it is of critical importance that the federal government be widely perceived as doing all it can to respond to the situation through as wide a range of action as possible.
The key word in that quotation obviously is "perceived"- "perceived as doing all it can". In a lifetime of watching cynical moves by the Liberal government, even my jaw dropped a little over that one. They seem to be saying, "Do not watch my actions, just look at the press releases" from the cabinet ministers on the low road. We have a saying in the west about people like this: "There is no business like no business".
Of course, the government thinks there will be a political payoff for its "as wide a range of action as possible". First there is the travelling circus of cabinet ministers. 1 understand that actually a drought agreement was signed with Manitoba today. On the weekend there may be more agreements to be signed in Victoria when the ministers of transport and the agriculture ministers get together.
I would simply like to say that there is a better way, a way that would not alienate the west and play into the hands of such evident opportunists as the Saskatchewan Unionist Party, a party led by a former Conservative leader who would like nothing better than to see the federal government play partisan politics with the drought. Surely no government in Washington would be so cynical as to say that the federal government must be widely perceived as doing all it can to respond to the situation.
On this side of the House we say, "Let us get on with the agreement Saskatchewan signed with the federal government in 1977". That agreement needs revising in view of changed conditions. In 1977 there was a shortage of surface water, but this year the water table has help up well. In 1977 movement of feed from farm to farm was a big component, but this year there is little excess feed to move. The federal government has been advised of these conditions for some time through its drought committee, yet as late as yesterday the minister of agriculture in Saskatchewan received a telex from the minister in Ottawa indicating that discussions have been tentative to date and that no commitments to drought relief have been made by cabinet. Who know what miracles tomorrow might bring?
The proposed agreement of two weeks ago does not have all the answers, and 1 must say that the hon. member for Medicine Hat pointed out other solutions in his speech today. But I think the draft agreement which may, after all, become a reality shortly, has some of the answers, and I would like to commend them.
First is the purchase of alfalfa pellets which were surplus to export commitments and the storing of them for resale as needed.
The second is back-hauling of hay on cattle liners from Ontario.
The third is assuring retention of enough barley stocks to meet regional needs-and I am repeating some of the suggestions made by the hon. member for Medicine Hat.
The fourth is a commitment of no further feed grain sales to export markets until the impact of the drought is known.
The fifth is halting the movement of non-Wheat Board grains for two weeks to allow for assessment of prarie stocks.
The sixth is return of pelletized screenings from Thunder Bay or Vancouver that are excess to export commitments.
The seventh is to use provincial and federal wildlife preserves for grazing where possible.
May 30, 1980

The eighth is to assist in the transportation of cattle to those areas or to other available pasture.
The ninth is the implementation of a fodder and feed grain listing service.
The tenth is assistance to farmers in developing wells.
The eleventh is assistance in respect of dug-out pumping where necessary; and lastly, the twelfth is assistance in the development of municipal wells.
The wording of this motion is very apt. We do regret the lack of action, just as we have sometimes regretted the lack of action by the Conservatives in proposing alternatives. The minister has admitted that his department has long been alerted to the problem, but there has been no action. There has also been an approach taken to the drought that has been secretive and clothed in cynicism. The government's hesitancy to commit itself either to the Saskatchewan program or to commit funds to implement it makes us a little suspicious that the reason the government is holding off is to make the meeting in Victoria this weekend a big media event. Such an approach is inexcusable and will make all of this government's stalling tactics suspect and opportunistic.
In closing, I would like to point out half a dozen main areas where the government could help farmers to survive this impending or partial disaster if we get as much rain as we have in the last few days.
Let us have some concern for action in respect of livestock right now. Let us have some concern for the livestock industry on a long-term basis, such as the suggestion regarding a national meat authority. Let us put into place a continuous plan which can be called upon on very short notice to keep the whole agricultural industry going in times of drought. Let us put in place a credit system which will allow farmers to survive in stressing times. Let us get all the feed grains back under the Canadian Wheat Board so we can be sure we have the kind of information and control of grain movement we need. Let us not appear to do something about the drought situation; let us do something about it. Let us do something as a Parliament and not as a party attempting to impress the west.
The bible story of the seven lean years is being repeated in southern Sahara regions. We pride ourselves on our planning and on our technology, but that may not be enough if the rains do not come. Let us approach this crisis as a nation should, and be prepared to do as a good government should.

Indeed, I found that the description of the drought, this very serious matter that concerns all Canadians, given by the hon. member for Medicine Hat was one that was accurate; it was reasonable and it was sincere, and that from a man who has basically experienced droughts in the past and foresees the dangers that might face his people in Alberta, particularly the cattlemen, if this situation continues.

speechtext:
1 would be more than willing to go and meet the people in that area so they can discuss that with me; but I know that no one could better represent those constituencies than those who have been elected.
When 1 heard the member for Prince Albert, I could not help but remember that 1 was in Prince Albert on several occasions, as he knows, and I know how very interested he is in the ambitions and the needs of his people there. When he said that there should be something done as a Parliament, he is entirely right.
Before answering the very positive recommendations that both he and the hon. member for Medicine Hat have suggested to this House, let me bring the members of this House and the people of Canada up to date on basically what the situation is in relation to the drought in Canada right now. There is no question about it, the drought in western Canada and in northwestern Ontario also is critical and requires immediate federal action. In that regard I completely associate myself with the remarks of both the hon. member for Prince Albert and the hon. member for Medicine Hat.
At this time the Department of Agriculture is preparing an immediate contingency paper. The task force is in action right now. Indeed, later on this afternoon the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) will be speaking on this subject. At the noon break he is meeting with members of the Department of Agriculture in order that he can bring members up to date on the latest developments in this particular regard.
As the hon. member for Medicine Hat says, indeed, serious drought conditions exist on the prairies as well as in the United States and in northwestern Ontario. Pasture and hay crop conditions are poor. The supply of cattle feed for this summer is critical and of growing concern. Indeed, the few drops of rain in Alberta may have made it possible for some cattlemen to recover, but, indeed, the short grass situation is critical.
We do not know the consequences if the cattlemen were put in the situation where they had to dump all their beef on the

May 30, 1980
Agricultural Drought
market with a subsequent drop in price and the difficulty they would face in restarting their herds. I assure this House that 1 will bring to the attention of the Minister of Finance the very serious and very adequate and fair tax proposals the hon. member for Medicine Hat has put forward today. As he knows, I also sit on the finance committee of the House and I intend to assist him and associate myself with his demands, because members of this House, even if they do not have a farm in their ridings, are aware of the concerns of the cattlemen of this country.
Water supplies in major streams, lakes and underground are deteriorating, but the information we have is that they are still expected to be adequate to meet requirements up until perhaps the end of the summer of 1980.
Again I agree with the hon. member for Prince Albert when he says that immediate action should be taken to assist in the drilling of wells, and to assist also in the drilling of municipal wells. Later on this afternoon one of our speakers will explain to the House and the people of Canada the very practical and concrete measures taken by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion to basically assist and put some sort of irrigation system in place in the west.
However, I understand sufficient soil moisture generally exists for the germination of crops. The situation, as I understand it, is more serious for the cattlemen because the grain farmer does at least have crop insurance and a stabilization scheme.
For this reason 1 should like to address my attention now to the situation of the cattlemen. Recently the cattlemen came before the finance committee and complained about clauses in the Bank Act which they felt were inadequate to meet their needs. Members opposite made serious representations on their behalf and I was there with several members from our side to support their plea.
Basically, the problem we face is the absence of rain, and all the programs we can develop on this side of the House with the assistance and positive co-operation of members opposite will not bring rain. So there are several propositions. The tax proposal will not solve the problem immediately though it will certainly alleviate the concerns of the farmer. Another possibility which was mentioned was the reduction of beef imports to give farmers an assurance that at least they would have a market in which to sell.
Another point which was raised by the hon. member for Prince Albert-I am not sure I agree with it-was that we should begin transporting hay from the east to the west. From the little knowledge 1 have, I believe the cost would be such as to be almost prohibitive. I will, maybe, ask the people in the departments of transport and agriculture to put together a package to find out basically whether the idea is feasible or not. When the hon. member talks about sufficient stocks of barley, I agree with him. There is no question we shall have sufficient stocks of barley because in the parts of Saskatchewan 1 know drought is something which could happen any
year. Basically, the weather in southern Saskatchewan and in the area around Medicine Hat is dry.
I agree with the hon. member from Prince Albert: now is the time to do something. The hon. member put forward some 12 concrete proposals for immediate action and five long-term proposals. I was not able to make note of all of them but 1 certainly intend in the near future to have a conversation with him and to make sure that his representations are brought to the attention of the departments of agriculture and finance. I will make sure that this is done.
However, I was disappointed with the hon. member when he said that we on this side wanted to make political gains out of this situation. I would point out that there is not likely to be an election for four years and that there are no political gains for us to make in the short term. The hon. member should understand that we, especially those of us who have just been through a referendum, believe we are here to represent the whole country and we do not want to make short-term political gains. Absence of rain is something we can do nothing about.
The hon. member has put forward strong and concrete proposals. But to suggest we want to make a big show for June 3 and 4 in Victoria is completely wrong. That is unfair and 1 am disappointed with the hon. member for making that suggestion. 1 can only think that some member of his staff wrote it and that he accidentally read it to the House. As the hon. member knows very well, we have the situation out west at heart. I hope that this afternnon when the Minister of Transport meets with officials from the Department of Agriculture and others about what the Department of Regional Economic Expansion will be doing, we shall be able to provide more satisfactory answers.
I also want to talk to the hon. member about the suggestion that somehow the Department of Agriculture did not agree with, changed its mind, withdrew or deceived the government of Saskatchewan and its minister of agriculture by saying one day that there was a deal and on another day that there was not a deal. From what I understand, according to information provided to me by officials of the Department of Agriculture and as repeated in this House by the Minister of Agriculture, an agreement was being discussed at a meeting of deputy ministers but nothing formal was decided. We have not turned down Mr. MacMurchy's request at this time. All we have done basically is say this: "Mr. MacMurchy has talked to our deputy minister, Mr. Lussier, Mr. Lussier has talked to the Minister of Agriculture, who in turn brought the matter to the attention of the various ministers who are concerned and who will bring it to the attention of cabinet". This is very different from saying we have rejected the request.
In a situation like this there can be no politics. We are here as a nation. That is why, when the provinces get together and talk to our department, 1 would never accuse them of trying to make politics. Basically, everyone is concerned about this situation. Concrete proposals have been made and we will act on them in the belief that the plight of the western farmer is of interest to all the nation.
May 30, 1980

Agricultural Drought
I intend to go out west several times next year and in the years to come to meet with more of the prairie farmers. I think a suggestion which could be acted upon quickly would be to have the members of the agriculture committee travel across Canada and listen to the representations of the kind which were made by the hon. member for Medicine Hat and by the hon. member for Prince Albert. They could talk to the farmers and to representatives of the Cattlemen's Association to make sure that the crisis situation which has arisen this year, a situation we experienced partially in 1977, in 1960-61 and for ten years in the thirties, will not continue. I cannot but believe that we on this side of the House, especially those who have just finished a very strong battle in Quebec, will be willing and understanding and ready to go to bat with our ministers and our officials who have the plight of the western farmers at heart. The hon. member may rest assured that this afternoon he will get precise and up-to-date information.
The hon. member mentioned an agreement made with the government of Manitoba. I am not aware of that agreement; maybe there is one. The Minister of Transport, at the meeting with officials, will have up-to-the-moment information.
The hon. member mentioned a big show in Victoria. Again,
1 am not aware of that. I am aware there is a meeting in Victoria but not a big show, a big political rally. That is not what it is about. What we intend to do is to take forceful action immediately. In 1977 we had a cabinet committee, an officials committee and a task force. This year that task force went into effect, met with the different farm organizations and met with the provincial organizations at the official level. It then made a report to the senior officials who then met with the deputy ministers. Now we are at the cabinet stage and with the help of the positive suggestions by the hon. members for Medicine Hat and Prince Albert we have the benefit of an even better and more complete file.
I am very pleased to have the occasion, in the absence of the Minister of Agriculture and his parliamentary secretary, as one, who represents a very rural riding in southern Montreal despite the fact that its name is Laprairie and that it does not have a single farm on it, to get up once again to talk about my concern for and my devotion to the cause of the prairie farmer.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT RESPONSE REGARDING AGRICULTURAL DROUGHT AND FOREST FIRE EMERGENCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member. 1 shall try to respect my 20-minute limit. I believe I can manage it. First of all, I should like to reiterate the excuses of the Minister'of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) who had to leave yesterday or this morning-I believe he left last night, in fact-to attend the World Food Conference in Tanzania, Africa. I know the minister would have liked to be in the House today.
Secondly, 1 want to say that the government is really grateful for the debate today and wishes to thank hon. members who are willing to take part in it. This debate obviously gives the opportunity of keeping the people of Canada informed about the present situation with regard to the drought in western Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the first part of my remarks which I obtained from the Department of Agriculture has to do with a description of the present weather situation in the west. Serious drought conditions continue, as we all know, to be experienced
1598

May 30, 1980
Agricultural Drought
across a large area of the prairie provinces and areas also in northwestern Ontario and the interior of British Columbia. The generally dry fall in 1979, below normal winter precipitation, and a hot, dry April and May have contributed to cause below normal moisture conditions. The moisture shortages range from critical to below normal.
The one bright spot in recent weeks, as the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) underlined this morning, has been rain in southern and some parts of central Alberta, but a lack of moisture is causing great hardship on many other people elsewhere.
The worst forest fire conditions on record are being experienced in the northern areas of western Canada and northwestern Ontario. Substantial damage has already been done and, as we all know, many people have had to be taken by Armed Forces planes and personnel from their homes as fires threaten. I am glad to be able to tell hon. members that many of these residents of our northern areas now have returned to their homes. Cooler, damp weather has helped put out some of the fires and reduced the fire hazard. But it is recognized that the over-all dry conditions across the prairies continue and are threatening to have a serious effect on agricultural production.
1 share the concern of some hon. members that the cereal crop in western Canada is in jeopardy because of low moisture reserves in the soil and in some areas a total lack of rainfall. I am told that it is still not too late for the wheat crop to recover and to provide its usual bounty. Timely rains could indeed turn the situation around for grain producers. But there is no question that if the present weather conditions prevail for very much longer, there will be an increasing number of short and long-term problems developing. In a nutshell, the situation is serious but not yet critical. We all pray and hope that it will not become critical.
Livestock producers have been the first to be affected. Increasing demands placed on already short feed supplies and local water supplies are causing great concern. Livestock and feed, when available, must be transported long distances. There is also a concern that some cattlemen may have to sell off their herds if feed becomes scarce.
There is no question that the drought situation is more serious in some respects than the dry conditions of 1977. It is far more widespread, covering a very large area of western Canada.
What, then, is being done? First, the government has been continuing to monitor the situation most carefully. Cabinet members have met their provincial counterparts, and senior officials within various government departments have consulted with provincial officials.
In 1977, the last year drought conditions existed on the prairies, cabinet approved the formation of a federal task force on drought. The task force was charged with the responsibility of assembling information, recommending government action
and co-ordinating programs aimed at alleviating the situation for western farmers.
I would like to make it clear to my hon. friends that the task force was not simply a one-shot affair. It has continued in existence in Regina since 1977 and has been meeting regularly. In fact, it has regularly reported moisture conditions to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. De Bane), and these reports have been made public.
This morning, the hon. member for Medicine Hat suggested that the names of the members of the task force be made public. If I am permitted, Mr. Speaker, I will do so now. The chairman is Mr. V. O. Coffey from Agriculture Canada; the secretary is Mr. D. James, a representative of DREE in Saskatchewan. The members are as follows: Mr. J. C. Lowe, representing Agriculture Canada; Mr. J. R. Lane, DREE, Saskatchewan; Mr. G. S. Brown, PFRA-as hon. members know, that is part of DREE; Mr. D. A. Davis, Environment, Regina; Mr. W. H. Willis, EPC, Winnipeg; and Mr. W. L. Tucker, Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, Winnipeg.
There is an interdepartmental steering committee working from Ottawa which is chaired by Mr. Mike Heeney of Agriculture Canada. I would like to thank these people for their participation in this task force.
As I was saying, the task force is a permanent institution now and it met last in Regina on May 16 with senior officials from the provincial governments of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. It was agreed at this meeting that a drought of major proportions was developing, and that joint federal-provincial action was urgently needed. Action plans were presented as soon as possible to the respective governments of task force members for consideration and implementation.
As a result of this meeting, all hon. members would have received last week a memorandum of information from the Minister of Agriculture providing the most up-to-date information possible on the drought situation. Similar information has been made available regularly to western farmers and to the members of Parliament through media releases from Agriculture Canada.
Today marks the reinstatement of a weekly drought report first initiated in 1977 during dry conditions. The report which hon. members will receive on Monday morning not only provides current information on weather conditions, but also provides some predictions as to what these conditions mean to prairie farmers. That report is widely available in both print form and by radio across the prairies.
At lunch time I managed to get an advance copy of the report. If members want to know what the situation is in their particular region-it is divided into geographical areas-if they would get in touch with me, I will let them see it.
Just last weekend the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy), the Minister of State for Economic Development and Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board toured the most seriously
si
May 30, 1980

affected areas of the prairies to gain first hand information on the situation. They met in Regina with task force officials. A draft paper recommending certain federal action to alleviate hardships caused by the dry weather was also studied by ministers at that time.
Task force officials worked out details this week. Just three days ago a meeting of senior federal officials was held in Ottawa to review these details and to make specific recommendations. These recommendations for action will be placed before cabinet for decision next week, Mr. Speaker, and I can assure hon. members that the matter will receive the highest priority. Detailed federal plans aimed at assisting producers on the prairie provinces will be announced as soon as possible after cabinet has made its decision.
The Minister of Agriculture was sort of chastised this morning for saying that he could not act as rapidly as others thought he should. I thought he stood on very good ground. The proper way of doing these things is for the minister-or any one of them-to go to cabinet first to get authorization for whatever he wants to do before proceeding with an announcement. 1 thought some of my friends were unfair to the very friendly and able Minister of Agriculture. So I stand up today to support him.
This document, the one I referred to as coming before cabinet next week, will address the most urgent part of this situation, that is, pasture and feed for cattle. It will cover possible moves on the feasibility of transportation of cattle feed and transportation of cattle to pasture. It will make decisions about that. It will also address the possibility of accelerating programs for the provision of water facilities, not that these programs are entirely new-we all know that they exist-but there is a possibility they could be accelerated. This is the sort of thing the document will be about and it is on what the cabinet will base its decision. Therefore, my hon. friends will have their curiosity satisfied by this announcement next week.
In the meantime, the task force members and senior federal officials are considering further government action should the drought continue. The drought situation can change very rapidly, we know that, but the government will be in a position to react to a worsening situation very rapidly if it becomes necessary.
The hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) seemed to make a great to do about a meeting to be held on June 3 in Victoria. I think he was implying that this was another one of those Liberal conspiracies to get maximum press coverage. 1 just want to tell him that I will be at that meeting. The meeting was called to discuss grain transportation. A minister from one of the provinces informed the chairman of that group that he would like to discuss drought conditions should they not improve in the meantime. It was by provincial action that the subject of drought was brought up as a possibility for discussion at the meeting in Victoria. My friend might want to apologize or blush for having imputed motives that were not there certainly in the first place.
Agricultural Drought
So that there is no confusion as to the action the government already has taken to handle the drought situation on a continuing basis, I would like rapidly to review some of its programs and other activities. While the emergency measures to be considered by cabinet will be geared to answer specific needs for this year, there exist other measures that have been in place, in some cases for decades. 1 will mention just three.
First, ever since the dust bowl days of the 1930s, Agriculture Canada's research stations in the western provinces have laboured to provide farmers with new tools, management techniques and different crop varieties to combat the odds of farming in what is naturally a dry land area. This has been met with great success and international acclaim.
The second measure I want to mention is crop insurance programs, half the premiums for which are paid by the federal government. This is another way in which prairie farmers can protect their investment in the land. About 80,000 western grain farmers have purchased $1.5 billion worth of crop insurance protection for this year. The federal government will contribute about $73 million to premiums in the western provinces. The government also assists provinces through reinsurance programs when indemnities greatly exceed reserves. This is another measure that exists, and I am sure hon. members are aware of it and others. 1 just mention them as a record of the system that has been built throughout the years to anticipate situations like the one now confronting us.
Third, the Western Grain Stabilization Act provides income protection should poor crop yields result in poor market returns and reduced net cash flows. Some 74 per cent of all rain producers on the prairies are part of this program.
As I have said, our immediate concern is for the livestock producers who are suffering the most from soil moisture conditions at the present time. I can assure hon. members that government emergency action will recognize that fact. The selling off of cattle and subsequent reduction in western breeding herds must be prevented, as was stated by some members this morning.
To sum up, the government stands ready to institute whatever action is needed to help producers as well as residents of western Canada should the drought conditions continue much longer. 1 repeat that the situation is a very serious one, but it has not reached critical proportions. Hopefully it will not. However, to react to the present serious situation, the government will make announcements next week.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Gatineau (Mr. Cousineau) for assisting in this debate. I was pleased with the remarks of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) in that we have finally had a statement in the House from the government on a very serious problem that faces the three prairie provinces, part of British Columbia and part of Ontario.
If I am critical of the Liberal government, it is because of the lenght of time it has taken them to realize the problems that drought is causing individuals. It may not be of a huge proportion in some minds, but this drought, this disaster, this quirk of Mother Nature, is of huge proportions in their personal lives.
1 would like to try and express this in a way a friend of mine from southern Saskatchewan does. When we are talking about drought, some people say drought, some people say "drouth". I don't care what you say, it's damned dry in Saskatchewan right now. We, and I am talking about men, governments and human resources, all believe that rain will come and that the "Man upstairs" looks after us; but we cannot wait for help because we need to have help now.
I would like to draw attention to some of the problems that we have, some of which were mentioned earlier by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) and the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo). The task force that was organized in 1977 and which is still in existence is made up of those mentioned by the minister, very capable and responsible members of our bureaucracy. I have a great deal of empathy for those members. They come up with programs that are of great assistance. The only problem with the programs is that they cost money. These hard working civil servants go out and try to provide the answers. When they come back and ask for money to carry out the programs that will assist those suffering from this drought, they find that this is where the problem lies. It is not a problem of finding the answers. We have very capable people who have provided the answers. The problem lies with whether this government is committed, believes and is concerned that it will find the money or the resources to give the assistance that is needed in western Canada, not tomorrow and not next week but now.
The Minister of Transport took exception to one of the previous speakers' comment that things should be done quickly and should be done now. However, I would draw his attention to some of the things the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) said when we were in government and he in opposition. He said it was a shame that agriculture was not represented properly in the Clark cabinet, that the then minister of agriculture was not a member of the inner cabinet. What he forgot to recognize as important is that that minister was a member of Treasury Board. When you are a member of
Treasury Board, you have ample opportunity to get fast decisions on problems concerning agriculture. The present Minister of Agriculture is not a member of Treasury Board. That is why we have to wait so long before competent and precise help is given to those in western Canada.
I wish to bring to the attention of the House the supplies that we have in western Canada to give us assistance with this problem. It has been mentioned that screenings should be used to supplement feed. There are people in my constituency who have turned cattle out on to grass. When they did that, they also had to feed them. They have to grind, chop and supply feed in addition to grass for the cattle. The reason for that is that they were breeding stock.
I would like to correct an impression that may have been left by the hon. member for Prince Albert about a statement made by the hon. member for Medicine Hat, who has long been recognized in the cattle industry and other industries in Canada as a very knowledgeable person. He did not say that we should sell off half of our breeding stock. What the hon. member for Medicine Hat said was that in some instances farmers and ranchers are selling up to half their breeding stock. Selling half their breeding stock is giving away their ability to earn a living. It takes away the ability of families, ranchers and farmers to earn a living. They can no longer earn a living unless they have their breeding stock. The only cash they get comes when calves are dropped, grassed and then fed. When you give away or are forced to sell part of your ability to earn a living, it is not a small matter; it is critical, and it is critical right now.
We have very small supplies of screenings in western Canada. As a matter of fact, my information is that at the most we have available now only 450 tonnes of screenings, which would not make a significant difference, considering the numbers of cattle which will have to be fed. A problem arises because of a formula called the corn competitive formula which says that barley sold within Canada should be based on the price, the energy efficiency and the price of equal efficiency of corn which comes in from the United States.
What it is doing now is that the cattlemen who are in need of feed are buying barley from the Canadian Wheat Board stocks because they can buy it cheaper from the Canadian Wheat Board stocks under the corn competitive formula than they can buy it non-board, from elevator companies or from their neighbours, their farmer and rancher friends.
The other thing that is going to develop is a shortage of barley for both areas. There are approximately 200,000 tonnes of barley on-farm in western Canada, and it will not be sold to the Canadian Wheat Board. It will not be sold on quota until the price comes up 40 cents or 50 cents or until a quota opens up which will allow it to be sold. These are some of the problems.
Long before my time the PFRA served the people of western Canada well. It has the interest of the people of western Canada at heart at all times, but right now on PFRA pastures
May 30, 1980

there are aproximately 190,000 head of cattle. Officials of that agency say that the optimum expectation is that grass and water-one or the other and in some cases both-will dry up by the end of June. These cattle are going to have to be taken out of the pastures and put on feed in feedlots on farms. This is an additional burden, but farmers and ranchers will do this to save their breeding stock.
1 am aware of the deep program of the PFRA, but 1 would like to draw the attention of the House and the minister to the fact that in this year of drought there have only been 251 deep wells drilled in western Canada as of May 28. This compares with the year 1977-and I realize we are only at the end of May-when there were 4,059 deep wells dug by the PFRA or with the assistance of the PFRA. 1 commend this program of the PFRA, but I also ask that the government provide the monetary means-the dollars-so that this agency can function.
There are some other things I would like to mention, but one thing I want particularly to bring to the attention of the House is the suggestion the hon. member for Medicine Hat made regarding an annual income averaging program for cattlemen and farmers who are forced, through no fault of their own but because of the quirk of Mother Nature, to sell their stock. The hon. member for Prince Albert said that this would not help the small operator, but I think it should be drawn to his attention that a small operator with 30 or 40 head of breeding stock has a total investment of anywhere from $35,000 to $45,000.
If he is forced to sell half of that, he will pay anywhere from 30 per cent to 40 per cent of the proceeds in income tax. Five-year averaging does not help. 1 do not know how the hon. member for Prince Albert would feel were he a farmer or had he experience on the farm, but 1 would not want to have to sell my cows. I would not want to have to give away 40 per cent even on 20 head of cattle. Larger operators whose cattle are on short grass have no back-up. They rely on grass to produce the calves they sell for income. The smaller farmer is usually a mixed farmer. He has access to straw, feed grains and cereal grains, so that he can get through. It will cost him more, but he will get through. I would like to draw that to the attention of the House.
Mention has been made of programs which are available to producers in western Canada when it comes to crop insurance. The minister stated that there are about 80,000 farmers involved in the crop insurance program. We recognize that that program is funded partially by the federal government and by the provincial governments, but I must add that the people who buy it, the producers, also fund it. There are 80,000 farmers involved in this program, but there are 150,000 permit book holders in western Canada. That means that just s little over half of the farmers are protected under the crop insurance program.
Western grain stabilization was mentioned. This is a program which is of assistance, but again only 70 per cent of the producers participate in that program.
Agricultural Drought
One problem in the cattle industry which is critical now is that if it does not rain within the next ten days, there will be a problem with cereal grain production. For the information of the minister, we are about a month ahead in our growing season in western Canada now compared with the average year. Ordinarily if there has been no rain by the first of June we do not panic, but crops have been in the ground for 30 days or 40 days. The germination is not so good. It really is not great. Gophers have to pack a lunch to travel across 100 acres. There is nothing to eat. We must have some feeling of concern for the grain producer right now. I agree that the situation is not as critical as it is for the cattleman because the cattleman is selling off his ability to earn an income.
Considering the expressions of good faith and good will by the government toward people in western Canada and all parts of Canada who are having a problem, I hope that it will again take a very strong look at income averaging in order to protect people who, again through no fault of their own, have been forced to sell parts of their cattle herds.
1 hope the Canadian Wheat Board will be instructed to guarantee a supply of feed grain on the prairies, but again let us keep in mind that the mandate of the Canadian Wheat Board is to export grain out of Canada. I know this is a problem, but I think there must be some way of getting around it.
We certainly hope there will be federal assistance given to the movement of cattle from western Canada to Ontario and Quebec. We had the assurance from our confreres in the Standing Committee on Agriculture yesterday that there is more than enough forage in Ontario and Quebec to assist in a small way in saving our breeding stock. We would like to see if a back haul could be originated to haul grain and hay back.
We hope that the government will look at a meat import law. That would not help in the drought, but it would help cattlemen and farmers have some faith in the industry of raising beef. Unless they have faith, and unless they know they are going to get a fair return for their sweat, they will sell their breeding herds and it is not just the cattlemen and the farmers who will suffer; every consumer in Canada will feel the effect within the next 18 to 24 months. We hope the government will take a strong look at placing the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Administration, or the act, under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Agriculture.

speechtext: Why not Transport?
