speechtext:
The minister suggests Transport. I will pass over that. The Minister of Transport is a busy man and I do not think he really needs anything else to keep him occupied.
The hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Deniger) said he had a feeling for western Canada and understands some of the problems there even if he does not have a farm. I recognize that, and there are other members on his side who have a similar approach. If the government is willing to take the steps which are needed along the lines of suggestions which have

May 30, 1980
Agricultural Drought
been put forward, it will renew faith in western Canada that the federal government does care about the region. But if steps are not taken, and taken soon, this belief will be very hard to maintain in western Canada. In contradiction to the view held by some people, I should like to say that the situation is critical now. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT RESPONSE REGARDING AGRICULTURAL DROUGHT AND FOREST FIRE EMERGENCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate although I regret the situation we are discussing is not a healthy one in terms of the western economy or the Canadian economy as a whole. It is very unpredictable. Today we might be talking about a very serious drought; tomorrow the rains may come and continue to fall and then, all of a sudden, the situation is fine and dandy.
This does not excuse the government from taking action. After all, the government has a responsibility here, as it indicated in the Speech from the Throne. Along with many other western members, 1 read that speech and heard it from the mouth of none other than the Governor General, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) recited to us in western Canada that we had a responsibility to indicate to the people in western Canada what the government was doing. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, how can we tell the people of western Canada what the government is doing if the government does not tell us what it intends to do?
If anyone doubts the seriousness of the drought, one has only to look back at past history. I can remember what happened in 1961. Not too many people have experienced drought conditions but I suppose that in my lifetime I experienced it also in the thirties as a boy. 1 did not understand the seriousness of it in those days. I was just a young shaver at the time and it really did not make much difference to me. One could have a lot of fun, even in the depression. You did not need much money to get by. You ate what was available, you did what everybody else did and you did not ask questions.
That was in the days when you did not require capital. Those were the days when you could feed a horse, turn it out to pasture for a couple of hours in the afternoon in the heat of the sun, and about four or five o'clock hook him up, drag him back out to the field and work again until late at night. But you cannot do that any more. So in terms of today's economy there is no comparison with the thirties, and 1 think we may as well forget about trying to make one because any time reference is made to the thirties it is such a foreign thing for everybody to understand. It is something for the CBC to recall whenever they want to drag out something about the prairies and western Canada.
Western Canada is not the prairies any more. Western Canada is far more than vast prairie dust bowls and so on. It is true there is the possibility of dust bowls and grave economic consequences. But the dust bowls are gone forever in terms of our agricultural approach and our ability to cope with them. Our ability to cope demands several factors. One of those is the ability to raise capital, and ability to raise capital depends
very much on the ability of the government to understand the consequences of what is happening today.
We have a far more serious problem than relates to only one province. Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, British Columbia and parts of Ontario are affected by drought. When I say parts of Ontario are affected, I am talking about the forest fire situation as it affects the northern area. If anybody doubts the consequences of forest fires in the northern parts of our country he has only to look at the value of the tourist dollar that produces an income to Canada. If ever Canada needed income from foreign capital, it needs it today. And if ever a government needed a jolt to make it understand the consequences of the folly of the financial policy it is pursuing it needs it now. It is oblivious to the fact that it is heading totally in the wrong direction in terms of deficits. The time to budget for deficits is when we have the one we are facing today, to pull us out of an economic recession.
Just look at what is reported in today's The Globe and Mail. If people in eastern Canada are not aware of the consequences of what is happening in western Canada, let them look at the Massey-Ferguson lay-offs which will reach 6,850. Do 1 need to say more? Who is it, Mr. Speaker, who buys the tractors? Who buys the combines? It is the people who have been complaining to their representatives in the House of Commons, and they are asking this government to outline a plan for coping with the situation.
The government announced they had a plan. They told us they had some sort of a task force. Where was it? Hidden in a cupboard? What was it doing? Studying itself-studying its navel, 1 guess. I do not know what it was doing. But the point is this: they did not indicate to the people most affected what they intended to do in the event of a serious situation developing. And it was developing very rapidly. Imagine the situation which existed when we started out this spring. Interest rates stood at 18 per cent. What were the producers to do? Were they to look up into the sky, say it was too dry, that interest was at 18 per cent and that the government didn't care? Were they to fold up?
They asked themselves these questions and said: "We don't care about the government, we don't care about the interest rates and we don't care about the weather. We are going to take our chances despite everything that everybody does to us because that is the nature of the farmer". But does that mean we have to say to them: "Yes, your're tough, but you withstood it before"?	[DOT]
You know, Mr. Speaker, there are such things as bankruptcies. We see the evidence of that. Once in a while the CBC comes out with a spectacular case. But we do not have to look at the spectacular cases. Businesses go under and nobody even notices them. All of a sudden a family farmer pulls out of a suitable home and goes into the city and becomes a statistic. We look down at the records later on and see that another farm has closed down.
May 30, 1980

What is important is net to come up with some grandiose scheme later on, but to deal with the situation right away. It is important to give them an indication of where you are going. They also have to make plans, whether or not the government knows it. Everybody in business who is affected by the income of the producers, whether they be cattle producers or other agricultural producers, has to make plans. You cannot imagine what it is like when you see grass which in the middle of June would normally be two feet high now only six inches high and very scarce. You can walk through it, you can see through it, you can see a blade of grass ten feet away. That is the kind of situation that you run into.
These people are not stupid, they know that they cannot carry their cattle through the winter, they know they have to unload them, and they know that every buyer in this country knows their situation. They know that the sooner they unload their cattle the better, because if they wait the situation will become worse. The government waits and waits, thinking that perhaps something will happen and it will not have to come through with anything.
With regard to the drought, the situation is not yet critical in my area. We hope that with some rainfall, perhaps even a bountiful crop might be produced. But let me tell the minister who sits over there who, although he is not responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board, is pinch-hitting for the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) at this time, that he had better take the message back that whatever kind of plan this task force may have for the cattle industry and for the grain industry, it had better be announced very quickly. Even an interim program is better than nothing.
Now let me go on to speak about the other industry affected, and that is the tourist industry. Elere I do not fault the federal government, and in fact I do not think it was through any action on the part of the federal government that the tourist industry has suffered. I want to give full marks to the Department of Regional Economic Expansion in so far as Saskatchewan is concerned, despite the credit which the province might want to take for itself, because people within the department foresaw the need for water bombers for Saskatchewan, and through DREE funding-perhaps the minister does not even know about this; in fact, 1 am sure he does not and I would like to fill him in on this-

speechtext:
Mattery goi you where you are.
Mri Korchinski: I want to give the department full marks because with the funds out of the northlands agreement, 60 per cent of the cost of the $1,500,000 program was provided to buy three water bombers for northern Saskatchewan. And what did the province of Saskatchewan do? They were not ready for the forest fires. They had a few tracker bombers which were on wheels but they could not scoop up the water as a water bomber can. The water bombers that were provided were equipped to cope with the situation. But they took their time, and of course the forest fires do not take time-whenever they come, they come.
Agricultural Drought
I want to give DREE full marks because they knew what the consequences would be to the tourist industry. The tourist industry depends a great deal upon Americans coming to northern Saskatchewan to fish. Tourist facilities in that area have had to be shut down, but the federal government had nothing to say to those people who heard nothing other than a bald announcement which came from the province of Saskatchewan. The province reversed a few statements here and there and implied that it was all to their credit, which is a lot of baloney, if I can use that term.

speechtext: It is parliamentary.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT RESPONSE REGARDING AGRICULTURAL DROUGHT AND FOREST FIRE EMERGENCY
speechtext:
The province was trying to take the credit for everything that was being done. I want to give the federal government credit in that regard, because at least the officials of DREE were aware of the need for water bombers. I do not know whether those three water bombers were sufficient for the amount of work that was being done.
Now I want to go back to the throne speech where the following statement was made:
It has been said in recent weeks that the three westernmost provinces have no elected voice in the governing of this country. That is not true. Parliament is the supreme law making assembly of Canada, and every Canadian is represented in the House of Commons by his or her duly elected member.
Like all of our colleagues in the House of Commons, you who represent the people of Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia have a responsibility to represent your constituents to the nation.
That is fair enough. In other words, the government is admonishing us, western representatives, that we have a job to do to inform the people. And yet when an industrial park was being opened up at La Ronge, what did the minister and his department do? It did not matter that I as the elected representative for 22 years-was not invited on the occasion, but they even denied me the opportunity to tell the people about what the federal government was going to do.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT RESPONSE REGARDING AGRICULTURAL DROUGHT AND FOREST FIRE EMERGENCY
speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT RESPONSE REGARDING AGRICULTURAL DROUGHT AND FOREST FIRE EMERGENCY
speechtext:
They denied me that opportunity, but they invited everyone else. They admonish me, they lecture me, and they tell me what my role as an MP is, and then when the opportunity arises they deny me the chance to play that role. It does not really matter because they have done that to me before and yet I am here. I would have told them the same thing I am telling them now. I give them credit where credit is due, if there is any credit due, but at the same time they deny me the opportunity to make information available to the people. That is what the resolution is all about, and that is what we are asking for. We ask for information about what the government is doing about the drought as it applies to dairy producers, beef producers, grain producers and the tourist industry.
Mr. Speaker, I do not think I need to say much more, but let me tell you that in my area, in Cumberland House, there are marshes-it is marshland area-and despite the droughts in western Canada we can grow great amounts of feed in that area. In 1961 when everywhere else there was no feed, we in

May 30, 1980
Agricultural Drought
Cumberland Elouse grew it and made it available. We had a trucking program to bring the feed to the southern parts of the country. Now it will be available there because the marshlands still exist. The land is flooded and grass will grow there. There are many other areas in the province that have similar programs in existence where feed will be available. They can be co-ordinated to benefit the beef industry so that cattle do not have to be slaughtered and producers will not have to make sacrifices at this time. It is an industry which is badly needed at this time.
I should like to say one other thing with regard to the effects of the forest fires in the province of Saskatchewan. The forest products industry in the province is about to abandon some of its operations. The fires have ravaged many parts of the province through the Hudson Bay area and around La Ronge in the north, a prime producing area where no less than three plants, to say the least, will be closing their operation. They will be using the excuse that it was high interest rates and everything else, but in reality the reason for their closure will be partly because they were not ready to cope with the forest fire situation.
The federal government has now reached a point where it requires $14 billion for its deficit position. That is an increase from the $11.5 billion which we projected. The federal government will never be in a position to help western Canada at this particular time, or maybe another area at another time, because of the monetary policies it is pursuing.
The other day I suggested that the Bank of Canada should take into account the drought in western Canada and its effect upon the economy. I was swept aside by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), but a few days later I saw a headline in The Globe and Mail which indicated that Ontario is affected. I am not a strange soothsayer. I do not have any way of knowing or predicting that certain things will happen, but I know if things are happening in one place that it will affect another place. All it takes is a little common sense on the part of the government. I ask the government to give us as much information as possible. The grain producers, the cattle producers, the tourist industry and the lumber industry in western Canada are capable of coping with difficult situations. They are intelligent people, but they must be given information so that they will know what the government is prepared to do and how far the government is prepared to go, and they will carry the rest.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT RESPONSE REGARDING AGRICULTURAL DROUGHT AND FOREST FIRE EMERGENCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to join my colleagues in this House to talk about the drought conditions in western Canada. Serious drought conditions affect a large part of the prairie provinces, certain areas of northern Ontario and British Columbia. A generally dry fall, below normal winter precipitation and a very hot and dry April and May have contributed to the present situation.
Moisture conditions range from low to average and the situation is critical.
The one bright spot in recent weeks has been rain in southern and some parts of central Alberta but a lack of moisture is also causing great hardship elsewhere. The northern prairies and northwestern Ontario are now having the worst forest fires ever recorded. Substantial damage has already been done and, as hon. members undoubtedly know, many people have been evacuated by the armed forces because of the threat those fires represent. Fortunately, most of these residents now have returned home. Cooler damp weather temperatures has helped put out some of the fires that were raging and reduced the fire hazard. However, the over-all dry conditions across the prairies continue and seriously threaten agricultural production.
I share the concern of my colleagues representing certain western areas that the cereal crop is in jeopardy because of low moisture reserves in the soil and a total lack of rainfall. But I am told it is still not too late for the wheat crop and yields could still be excellent if it rains and continues to rain as it has been doing in certain areas recently. But there is no question that if present weather conditions prevail we will face short and long-term problems. Livestock producers were the first to be affected. Because of increasing demands we can expect cattle feed shortages. In certain regions, the drop in water supplies also poses serious problems. Livestock and feed, when available, have to be transported over long distances. Also, cattlemen may have to sell off their herds if feed becomes scarce.
There is no question that the present situation is more serious in some aspects than the problems which existed in 1977. The problem has much greater proportions than three years ago. The government is monitoring the situation most carefully. In 1977, cabinet approved the formation of a special task force on drought whose mandate was to assemble information and make recommendations to government, besides co-ordinating various programs to alleviate the situation out west. The task force is still active and continues to meet. They met recently in Regina, on May 16 to be precise, with Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba senior government officials. According to the task force, we are facing a serious drought and the federal and provincial governments must be prepared to take immediate action.
During the last weekend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy), and also both ministers of state responsible for economic development and for the Canadian Wheat Board visited the most affected areas to see for themselves the extent of the problem. At the same time, they considered a working paper proposing that some measures be adopted by the federal government. A special committee has prepared the particulars of those proposals only three days ago. Those recommendations will be submitted to cabinet which should make a deci-

May 30, 1980

sion soon. In the meantime, the task force and the senior officials will continue to co-ordinate the goverment's action if the drought were to continue. The situation could improve quickly, but the government must be prepared to act as quickly as possible if things were to get worse. Not only have action plans been provided but I am convinced as all members in this House that the government will act in time and effectively to give assistance to western farmers.
It is important that decisions taken in those circumstances be the best possible. I believe that negative criticism would be contrary to the best interests of farmers and consumers alike. However, Mr. Speaker, we should refrain from dramatizing so as to avoid useless panic. Rain has fallen in some areas and yesterday we were informed that in some specific areas, four inches of rain had fallen, three inches in others and one inch elsewhere. Let us hope that the rain will greatly improve the grazing areas so that cattle may feed properly. Let us hope that this will continue and let us search for practical short, medium and long-term solutions because this drought could seriously impair western Canada's economy.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT RESPONSE REGARDING AGRICULTURAL DROUGHT AND FOREST FIRE EMERGENCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise today realizing that in my area we did get the first rains this year over the weekend, much needed rains, because, as the hon. member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight), said, much of the crop had been in the ground for 30 to 40 days and had been germinating sporadically. In the lower areas germination was taking place, and in the higher areas of fields there was no germination. This would have resulted in a very uneven crop and grain of very poor quality this fall. However, we did get the rain and I now am pleased to say that most of my farmers are saying germination is taking place across all of the fields.
This does not alleviate the problem regarding pasture lands in the west part of the ridings of Wetaskiwin, Red Deer and, I suspect, Vegreville, Bow River and Crowfoot. The pasture lands and hay lands are not growing. The only plants growing are the deep rooted alfalfa plants, which are already coming into bloom and should be cut one month before we generally go out and make the first cut of that hay for the year. This is disturbing.
1 am also concerned that many of the ranchers and farmers in the area raising cattle, because the pastures grass did not grow this spring, were forced to turn their cattle out on their hay fields to keep them going long enough until the pasture lands could get a bit of a foothold so that the pasture lands could hold the cattle through the fall when maybe some grain lands and straw would become available.
The very serious problem of drought has really affected most seriously now, and will continue to do so, feed for the cattle on the prairies, and that is something we have to turn our attention to as a Parliament.
Agricultural Drought
As I looked at the act which was brought forward by the government in 1935 to deal with drought I found that it had remained in its same form since that time. It has never been amended. Obviously it was well thought out by those who brought it forward at that time. We have found that because of that it has served as well since 1935 when first brought forward in this House. I refer to the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act.
I looked back at the debates of that time as I felt people then had just been through a most serious drought and surely we might be able to learn a lot from history. We may find ourselves in a recurring situation. Many of the things we should have been doing through the years were brought up at that time in 1935, and they have not changed.
I noted that the then minister in 1935, Mr. Weir, when bringing forward the act stated a number of policies that DREE should consider. One of those policies was to set up small areas, sort of experimental plots. He considered they should be a township in size and there should be three in Saskatchewan, one in Alberta, and one in Manitoba. The purpose was to develop grasses and grains that were hardy in drought conditions. There was also to be a tree-planting program to help farmers in the conservation of water. These were practical educational plots for farmers suggested by the scientists of that time who were capable of producing drought resistant plants, shelter belts, and the types of farming necessary in drought conditions.
I do not know what has happened to that program. I do not believe these experimental township plots are now in existence. Perhaps there is no need for them to exist, but surely with our modern techniques we must still learn the proper methods of farming when water is in short supply. If we look back to those records we might find that some of those techniques can still be applied today. Some of those crops could still be planted today in our pasture lands. We should bring these methods forward and make them available to farmers who may now have to experience similar weather conditions.
Many members of Parliament who spoke at that time talked about less water available than they had known in previous experience. As I look at my farm which has experienced the drought I can see the very same thing happening there today that happened to my ancestors back in the 1930s. Sloughs, as we call them, which contain water-we lament them because we have to go around them with our large equipment-have dried up. Usually they hold water which infiltrates the land around the slough and supplies water through capillary action to plants. As I have said, they are now dry. My brother seeded right through them this spring. I do not have a chance to work the farm any more since I am a member of Parliament, but I do keep watching on weekends to see what is happening. There is no water in them any more, largely as a result of very little snow this winter and no rain for 50 days this spring. The one and a half inches of rain we received are going to assist, but surely will be of no lasting value unless we get more.
Members back at that time talked about the very same thing. In fact one of the opposition members stated:

May 30, 1980
Agricultural Drought
The present situation presents an opportunity of guarding against a recurrence of these conditions. When limes were good people would not bother with rehabilitation, and that is why at the present time it creates a special opportunity with regard to the projects which we are now going forward.
They were talking then about preparing themselves for a situation that could come forward again in the future.
Another matter they talked about, which is essential, was the planting of shelter belts. When our forefathers came to this area they wanted to farm and they cut the trees. The rains came and they did not worry until the thirties when the rains did not come. The hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) said he was able to remember, and I am not, about the dust clouds and the drifting of the soil. Shelter belts can gather the snow in the winter as the winds drift it across the prairies, preserving that moisture in the areas where it is needed. In this way the snow does not drift onto the highways and into the towns where it is not needed. The shelter belts are absolutely essential. They also prevent the winds from gaining velocity and the soil does not drift as rapidly as it would otherwise.
Many members at that time spoke about the planting of trees. They suggested two things, shelter belts and plots. The advice accepted was in respect of shelter belts. 1 must commend the PFRA administration for what it has done since that time. I phoned the tree planting nursery at Indian Head, Saskatchewan. It was set up to do exactly this. I looked at some of the statistics and 1 was astonished. From 1935 to 1978 they have spent $11 million. In 1978 the nursery shipped its 400 millionth tree to prairie farmers in that region. In fact in 1977 when we experienced a bit of a drought, similar but not as severe as the one we are now experiencing, the demand for trees was greater than they could meet. They increased their yearly supply from six milliori in 1976 to 6.96 million in 1977, and they still had orders they were unable to fill. If there is anything we can learn from this it is that perhaps they need a larger grant so they can plant more trees to meet the demand.
As 1 looked at the records it seemed that each year, and 1 have the figures for 1974 to the present, their budget has been increasing, from $800,000 in 1974 to $1.2 million in 1977-78, which means that they are meeting as closely as possible the demands for this absolutely essential service to western farmers.
Another suggestion the hon. members spoke about at that time was in respect of measures for improving soil erosion controls, the provision of water storage, irrigation, and the better utilization of soil resources. They spoke about the withdrawal of submarginal lands from intensive farming to go over to pasture.
1 have some interest in renewable energy and it seems to me that the poplar tree that our scientists have developed, and which grows so rapidly, will be a valuable contribution. I know it is a relatively new tree, and some education would be required for farmers to learn the value of it over the traditional crops of alfalfa and other forage. It may sound odd to those of us who have farmed for years that we should switch submarginal lands from growing alfalfa to growing poplar trees. The tree grows so rapidly that, within two years, the farmer can take off 12 or 14 tons of matter for feed. He would not get close to that production with alfalfa. It grows very well on rocky, submarginal land, and it does not have to be harvested in dry weather. It has many advantages. Because it is deep rooted I suspect it would also be an advantage in a drought year such as this one. It is something on which agrologists might work with our farmers for submarginal lands in order that we can prepare ourselves for times like these.
We hope drought will not come very often, but when we go through a period of light rainfall we should utilize the technologies that are being developed which are essential to our agricultural industry. These trees can be developed to produce the energy required for that agriculture, because the product of the tree can be distilled into ethanol and methane gas. Those are two very welcome uses.
We welcome the way the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act has served us over the last 35 or 50 years. It set up some excellent programs from which we can still learn and which we should constantly study. It would have been useful in 1977, also this spring, and who knows when in the future? It set up four programs. One was for land use service to rehabilitate lands which were submarginal. The primary activities of the program were to be operational and administrative for a community pasture program. The second was a water development service. The hon. member for Kindersley-Lloydminster told us about the deep well drilling service which is very essential to the dry land ranching area of the prairies. In times of drought it means they can bring water up to fill their dug-outs.
I was out in western Canada last Friday, Mr. Speaker, and spoke to the minister of agriculture for Alberta. 1 asked him about the drought conditions there. He was very concerned and listed a number of programs that he was ready to put in place for the farmers of Alberta. One that he had already put to work was the filling of dug-outs. As there was no run-off from winter snows, the dug-outs were empty and there was nothing for the cattle to drink. Water had to be trucked in. If more deep water wells were drilled on the ranches under this program, I am sure it would cost less than it does to hire the trucks to haul water to fill the dug-outs. This is a very important program under the PFRA that should be going forward.
Another program for the distribution of seedlings and trees is operating very well. There is an irrigation demonstration facility at Outlook, Saskatchewan. The minister of agriculture in Alberta told me that irrigation is the solution, as the waters from the mountains flow, even under drought conditions.
The Alberta Heritage Trust Fund is often criticized but it is a pool of money that could be used for these programs, and $8.25 million has been set aside this year for irrigation head-works improvements, and $31.26 million for the expansion of the irrigation district. That is very welcome not only to the farmers of Alberta but to the farmers of western Canada
May 30, 1980

because alfalfa production in those irrigation lands can be used for alfalfa pellets and hay.
We are concerned about the province of Saskatchewan. The Diefenbaker Dam which was established for water resource management and hydroelectric development has run dry in the east ditch, and the Saskatchewan government has not brought forward plans for irrigation. That ditch should have been filled and put into use four or five years ago in order that the conditions we face today could be met. It is very important that more irrigation be planned for western Canada.
The third part of the PFRA program was to investigate plans, designs, and to be responsible for construction and maintenance of various works pertaining to water development, irrigation, and community infrastructure programs. This is more of a long-term planning procedure.
The last part of the PFRA program concerned administration, to provide for the internal management and programs related services for PFRA.
I think we can learn a lot from history, Mr. Speaker. That is where we find the best examples that members of Parliament and people in the committee of an earlier time felt had to be worked out. They have provided the examples for us. Surely we should continue with that excellent program, fostered by modren technology where possible. We could use some of the other scientific inventions such as plant breeding tools for such things as more drought resistant crops and poplar trees.
In summation, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote from a statement by the director of PFRA, Mr. Hill, contained in the 1977 annual report, as follows:
PFRA was uniquely able to render immediate aid to drought-threatened areas and was successful in administering relief programs in co-operation with provincial governments and other federal agencies. Valuable information obtained during the course of these activities led to the conclusion that the consequences of severe drought, which have occurred at random throughout the region, are not understood in terms of our present-day society, with its increasing water consumption and diversifying economic base.
The director tells us in this annual report that modern society has forgotten what it was like to live through seven, eight or nine years without rain and without snow in winter. We have now developed a society capable of wasting water day after day. Many of our farmers have not listened to their forefathers and are not using the techniques necessary for them to exist under dry land conditions. The government should take a lesson from what the director stated in this annual report given just after 1977 when there were sporadic drought conditions on the prairies.
I should like to turn now to a private member's motion which 1 introduced regarding the income averaging trust account. This is most important to the ranchers of my region and I am sure to ranchers of other regions which are similar. Sometimes they are compelled to sell their livestock because they cannot feed them. They then have money and no use for it, but find that one-quarter or one-third of it has to be paid in income tax-with which we all agree, of course. Surely we could bring forward a program to assist farmers at such times. In my motion which I put forward in February, 1979, I set out
Agricultural Drought
eight ways of doing that. The ideas are there. I would recommend that the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) look at these ideas. They are not just mine; most of them come from Peat Marwick Mitchell & Co. in a study prepared for the Department of Agriculture. These ideas could be used to set up a program and there would be no difficulty getting it past this side of the House, Mr. Speaker. I think it is essential that farmers be allowed this tool.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT RESPONSE REGARDING AGRICULTURAL DROUGHT AND FOREST FIRE EMERGENCY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT RESPONSE REGARDING AGRICULTURAL DROUGHT AND FOREST FIRE EMERGENCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise this afternoon to speak on the motion before the House.
That this House deeply regrets the government lack of response in this House of Commons to concern about the disastrous western agricultural drought and also the related forest fire emergency, and calls on the government to abandon its secretive approach and consult with members of Parliament of all parties in an open and in a forthright manner.
The farmers of the three prairie provinces are presently facing a very serious situation with possible consequences which could create economic havoc on a scale that has not been witnessed since the dust bowl days of 1930. While the majority of citizens in some of these provinces may be basking in the unseasonably hot weather, the farmer certainly is not. The livelihood of a number of producers is threatened, as well as the various businesses that service and process the farmers' goods.
A few areas in my own riding of Dauphin, such as Dauphin and McCreary, have received some rain within this last week, but other areas such as Roblin and Swan River are in desperate need of precipitation. In fact the majority of the provinces 30,000 farmers are worried that the drought may ruin their 1980 crops. There is widespread fear that the rye crop is already lost, for example. The Winkler weekly report states "-that emerged crop is turning yellow and may need to be reseeded". Certainly the situation is desperate in many places in the west.
We welcome, with appreciation, the department's reactivation of the 1977 drought task force. However, much more needs to be done. It is true, as has been mentioned, that there are certain programs in place that might be able to reduce the impact of whatever kind of weather conditions we have in the west, such as the crop insurance which covers some loss of crops. Also there is some protection under the Western Grain Stabilization Act. However, we would urge that the government act quickly in signing agreements, especially with the affected prairie provinces supporting drought assistance programs. We are reminded that Saskatchewan has submitted at least a ten point proposal for a drought assistance program which would be cost-shared between the province and the federal government. We would want action taken on programs like that, and similarly that action would be taken for Manitoba and other areas.

May 30, 1980
Agricultural Drought
I want to draw attention to what I consider to be six areas needing examination. There are six objectives that we should have when we look at the drought and related forest fire situation on the prairie provinces.
The first area that I wish to address is the area of feed and water supply assistance. One of our major objectives must be that we maintain the livestock herds in the west. There have been reports of some increase in the slaughtering of animals, and we would not want the slaughtering to affect the foundation herds. We must make sure, therefore, that we have a secure supply of feed even if it means that the feed must be brought from Ontario, or whether such things as feed pellets must be brought in from Thunder Bay. The foundation cow herds, the breeding stock, must be maintained, otherwise shortages of beef will occur along with a major disruption in the livestock industry in the future. Likewise, dairy herds must be protected.
To achieve this objective and to make sure that there is maintenance of livestock herds, we must take a look to see if there are some Crown lands available for emergency hay and pasture use. We would suggest also that perhaps there is some land which is under the auspices, at this stage, of the Wildlife Association of Canada, which should be examined. We should also make sure that there is an adequate feed supply for livestock in the area.
Similarly, when we take a look at some of the needs that we have in the west, 1 think we would want to see that the western livestock producer is treated in much the same way as the eastern livestock producer. In the east there is a domestic feed grain policy that guarantees supply to meet domestic needs. We would also want to ensure that something like that is true for the west. There should be a halt to export sales commitments of feed grains until we can be positive that there are adequate stocks on hand for the needs in the areas that might be affected by the drought.
There should be some direction given to the grain transportation authority to halt the allocation of cars to the movement of non-board feed grains from the prairies so that the needs of the drought-stricken areas might be met.
Perhaps there could also be a return of certain pelletized screenings from Thunder Bay or Vancouver that are in excess to our export commitments to make sure that the farmers in the west are able to supply their cattle with the necessary feed.
In connection with reaching the objective of maintaining our livestock herds, the other area 1 wanted to talk about is that of the provision of water. True, there is some assistance through the PFRA programs that already exist, but we may need to look at the need for irrigation of hay crop areas where there is such a feasibility, and also perhaps to take a good look at grants that might be available to farmers to assist them in developing water supplies that would be necessary to reach the objective that I have stated.
The second area I wanted to look at, in addition to the feed and water assistance areas that I have mentioned, is the whole area of transportation and storage assistance. There should be
some sort of policy there to make sure that, where necessary, the assistance is provided for the transportation of hay or feed grains to the required areas. In addition, through the hauling of feed there might be a necessity for moving cattle to alternative accommodation, moving cattle to pastures. Likewise, there is a major need for assistance for the farmers so they can be sure their cattle are provided for.
In the area of storage, the hon. member for Humboldt Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse), in his letter to the minister, mentioned that pending the outcome of the crop the federal government should implement a program for storing feed grains and forage in the prairie region in order to reduce the sell off of basic livestock herds. This is certainly critical to make sure that we are able to maintain the livestock herds in the west and to ensure that feedstocks will be available in the coming fall and winter. We want to make sure we protect our feed supplies now so that enough grain will be available to carry us through the upcoming winter.
The third area that we ought to look at with respect to the drought situation in the west is the necessity to alleviate the many problems that are faced by farmers. Basically I am looking at two areas when I look at the financial difficulties with which farmers are faced in the west. First is the area of income, and then comes the area of credit.
On the income side of the problem, we would want to see an initial price for wheat being kept at $4.25. The initial price as proposed for the wheat board grains for the 1980-81 crop year should be increased to the current level rather than dropped to $3.75. We want to make sure that we would discourage any selling off of grain before the end of July when this grain could more properly be held for feed and also for seed.
The federal government should also ensure that there is a final payment which is equal to the pre-embargo levels. Also, in the ara of stabilizing income we have always urged the implementation of national marketing systems for beef and hogs and for an expanded role for the Canadian Wheat Board. It is essential for the federal government to implement a stabilization plan for farm commodities which would reflect the net farm costs, because this whole area of income is definitely one of the problems and financial difficulties that farmers are facing in the west.
I also said that there is the whole area of credit, or the necessity for additional money. Many producers went into this drought faced with a heavy short-term debt load. There was a reduction in their cash flow. A potential crop failure could force many of them into bankruptcy. For this reason, the suggestions on extending credit amounts and guaranteeing the interest rates at minimal levels are a very necessary and integral rates at minimal levels are a very necessary and integal part of any program of drought relief. The federal government should set up some sort of emergency fund, perhaps through the Farm Credit Corporation, to allow for the transfer of short-term operating credit to longer-term loans at guaranteed low interest rates so that the necessary interim
May 30, 1980

financing could be there for those farmers who require it until the drought it over.
In this whole area of credit or money problems, there is also a need for individual moratoriums of farm debts. This likewise should be looked into by the Farm Credit Corporation. I am speaking on a moratorium on interest under such circumstances as might be requested by the federal government.
Another aspect that is of concern to us in the Dauphin constituency is that in the long run farmers do not start losing their land due to the non-payment of property taxes. There might be some need for assistance in this area as well when we look at the financial difficulties that would be facing the farmers.
Another area we want to look at, in addition to the third area of the money problems that I mentioned that farmers are faced with and that must be addressed in any sort of drought relief program, is the matter of providing information to farmers. Whatever types of programs are announced next week, we want to make sure that the farmers are aware of the programs, what exists, and what would be required for them. There definitely has to be some sort of co-ordination of information regarding the supplies and pastures that might be available for farmers experiencing feed shortages as drought conditions continue in the area. There needs to be some sort of monitoring of feed supplies and shortages, and certainly some sort of co-ordination with regard to the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Administration and other feed and pasture supplies.
There would be a need for information packages being provided to the farmers so that they would understand the types of programs that are available. For example, the Saskatchewan government has suggested that there is an immediate need for implementation of a fodder and feed grain listing service whereby farmers would be asked to list seed oats so that any available supplies may be used for seeding in June or July to provide green feed. This type of information service would be essential for any sort of successful program to cope with the very serious drought conditions that exist in the west.
I wish to spend a minute on the fire situation. In my constituency of Dauphin we have been living either in or adjacent to the fire problems on several fronts. On the northern side we have the Porcupine Mountains which have been affected by fire. This created a lot of fear among many of the residents there simply because in some cases they were forced to anticipate evacuation. Fortunately places like National Mills did not have to evacuate, but the situation indicated there was certainly a lack of response, especially in terms of the federal government.
When we think of the situation at Riding Mountain and Porcupine Mountain and the fire hazards created there, there was certainly no initiative on the part of the federal government to ensure that the required facilities and necessary arrangements were in place to deal with these fires, especially considering that there were American firefighting authorities who had been prepared to co-operate in battling and suppressing forest fires in areas such as Manitoba. The problem that these fires created underlines the need for acting more effi-
Agricultural Drought
ciently, and ensuring that in situations like this there is more of an input from members of Parliament who represent the area.
This leads me to the sixth point I want to mention dealing with any kind of drought program to be brought forward. This is the whole matter of consultation with members of Parliament. The government stated that it was prepared to work with members of Parliament. I have not had any contacts by the government with regard to the problems that might be faced in this whole drought and forest fire situation.
An indication of the lack of being able to deal with this problem is indicated in the announcement made this morning in Winnipeg with regard to the drought situation. This morning the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy), the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. De Bane), and the Manitoba government signed an agreement. Flowever, when you look at the impact this will have on the drought situation, there is only one sentence which suggests that some of the agreements as the apply to DREE might be implemented to deal with the drought situation. The whole problem of the drought appears to be merely an afterthought, as indicated by the type of agreement signed this morning.
Considering the pledge of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to work with the members of Parliament in the area, and considering the fact the government does not have representation in the west, I urge the government to ensure that there is a greater degree of consultation with members of Parliament so that, when faced with problems such as the drought situation and related forest fires, we can act expediently, effectively, and in such a way that will indicate to the people of the area that we are interested in their concerns and are prepared to deal with the problems they face.
1 welcome the opportunity this afternoon to express on behalf of my constituents our concern for the entire drought problem. I trust that the six points I mentioned in terms of implementing any programs relating to the drought will be taken into consideration so that we can be assured we will not face the prospects faced in years long gone by, but rather that the problems will be dealt with effectively.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph Ferguson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Small Businesses)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT RESPONSE REGARDING AGRICULTURAL DROUGHT AND FOREST FIRE EMERGENCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak in this debate as a farmer. Although I am from a different area of Canada than those which are so badly affected by this drought, I wish to place on record my concern for the people of western Canada, those in northern Ontario and other areas of the north where forest fires are a factor at the present time. In particular, my concern is for the cattlemen in the drylands and ranch areas of western Canada. I understand their problems because I, too, keep a herd of cattle. I am well aware of the reproductive cycle in the beef industry, from the time a heifer calf is born until that calf reaches maturity, conceives, and produces an offspring that grows to market weight. We are speaking here of a time frame of approximately three and a half years. I am well aware of what will happen if our beef herds are depleted, and the ensuing hardships that will be

May 30, 1980
Agricultural Drought
placed not only on our ranchers but on our economy in general. It is imperative that we keep our herd intact, and we must work for that protection in every manner possible.
I am concerned to about the grain farmers who face hardships, and those farmers in eastern Quebec and the Atlantic provinces who may not have adequate supplies of feed grains next winter and, therefore, may have to cut back their livestock and poultry operations.
1 well remember the drought of the early thirties that did extend into parts of Ontario and, more recently, the one in 1977 which existed to a lesser degree, particularly in the United States, in the State of Michigan which is not far from my riding, where a disaster did take place in terms of drought conditions at that time. I believe the type of help available today in Canada in situations like this is far superior to anything they have in the nation to the south of us.
1 indicated in committee yesterday that with respect to the area in which my family farm lies, in Lambton-Middlesex, we are in a narrow belt of land which does not receive the rainfall other farmers get just a few miles away. By a quirk of nature the storms and the rains seem to follow the Great Lakes. We happen to be in that area.
I phoned home today at lunch time. We finished planting our soya beans today. We have an excellent stand of corn and prospects to date are excellent. But conditions can change very, very rapidly. The weather patterns in our area appear to follow the lakes as I said, and the fact that we have to rely on moisture for our crops to sustain continued growth in our grain, our corn, soya beans and pastures, means we need to have some form of a contingency reserve of forage on hand. We always do this, but when we are planting our crops, too, we try to preserve the moisture in the subsoil reserve in the event that the normal rain does not materialize. Mr. Speaker, we fully realize the serious situation existing, particularly in B.C., Alberta, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and northern Ontario.
We look back in history. Drought is not new. There is a book, of course, which tells us of the wise ruler centuries ago who set aside grain reserves against a seven-year drought. But here in modern society perhaps it is time that we, too, examined the possibility of establishing food reserves of non-perishable products. We seem to have forgotten that history is a good teacher.
I fully agree with the hon. members from Medicine Hat and Prince Albert, who spoke first in this debate, that the situation is critical. The next few weeks will be indicative of the type of help needed. In all fairness, Mr. Speaker, these conditions did not just arrive over night. We all here should have recognized that the lack of snowfall last winter-much below normal- would result in dry land conditions to a greater degree than is normal. Perhaps we waited too long in the expectation of Mother Nature sending us the moisture required for bountiful crops, and it is obvious that in this regard we are all perhaps somewhat guilty. But as farmers, we are all optimists. We have to be, or we would not be involved in our sector of the
economy. Yet, as optimists, we have to think back, too, to where it is written some place:
He who watches the clouds neither reans nor sows
We have to be optimists. When we are engaged in that part of the economy, which is the greatest profession on earth, I trust that we can keep in mind the human suffering involved, the needs which must be met, and move in that direction to deal with the situations of distress as they develop, as the weather patterns unfold. At the present time the livestock industry is in distress and this alone is of real importance and of concern to all of us in Canada, regardless of whether we live in the east or the west. I agree that we must work together with all Canadians in an attempt to resolve these problems, and may I suggest the necessity of examining the feasibility of using some of our existing legislation to ensure that alfafa cubes and pellets are kept here in Canada. The legislation I refer to is the Export and Import Permits Act which was originally intended to be used in times of emergency.
We should make every effort to see that essential grains and screenings are kept in close proximity to the stricken areas, and that all forms of usable roughage feed be kept in western Canada. 1 fully realize that moving roughage from Ontario to the west is cost-prohibitive, but in emergency situations such as we face at the present time we must consider all possibilities. Every year there are countless numbers of trucks and cattle cars bringing cattle from western ranches to Ontario feed lots-we bring them in by the thousands-and I would like to ask the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin): do these trucks and rail cars go empty one way, or do they have a back haul? If there is no back haul, would it be possible to move some roughage on these empty units going west?
1 know that every year there are thousands of tons of clover and corn stover ploughed under, put back into the soil of Ontario farmers. There are thousands of tons of corn stover; in my area many farmers winter their cattle on corn stover alone, with no other additives than the protein additives and other nutrients. Could we examine this possibility rather than face the depletion of a vast portion of our national beef herd if conditions don't improve? I fully realize that at first glance, moving roughage seems quite illogical, but we must not leave any stone unturned in our effort to give help to our fellow Canadians.
To turn to another area, could we not examine the availability of irrigation equipment? Could such equipment not be sent out to those areas of western Canada where specialized crops are grown and where water is available? 1 fully realize that this is no help to the ranch areas or the grain-growing areas, but I refer to those areas where they grow vegetables and other specialized crops.
1 remember that several years ago the farmers of western Canada were unable to harvest their grain crops due to wet weather. But during the late autumn the grain combines were able to go on the fields and a large number of grain dryers were sent out to help dry the grain so that it could be stored safely and used as food and as livestock feed. Again 1 want to assure my western colleagues that we are willing to assist the
May 30, 1980

western farmers in this time of need. We sometimes teel quite helpless in situations such as this when, through no fault of the farmers or the governments at all levels, a national disaster occurs such as a drought, or maybe a flood, or an earthquake, or hurricane, to name but a few. We should remember that a drought situation is one which does not normally result in the loss of human life in North America, and for this we can be thankful. But we must realize the economic loss, the hardship and human suffering which will result from this natural disaster
1 have family relations across western Canada. Many of them are farmers and I well remember when I was young, before 1 went to school, going to Sunday school, and even though we ourselves were in a depression, bales of clothing were collected and Christmas presents were sent to help those in need. Again, 1 remember the disastrous drought which occurred here in the Ottawa Valley less than ten years ago. The governments helped those farmers through their times of need, and when I came into the airport here this morning I could not but help notice the contrast between the lush green valley here around the capital city and the parched fields I saw last week around Winnipeg. Certainly, as a farmer and as a member of this House, I am concerned and willing to help. 1 believe there have been several worthy suggestions made in the debate today. The statement by the Minister of Transport, the announcement of the task force, the discussion indicated for next week, have convinced me that the situation is being monitored closely-perhaps even more closely than some of us realize.
1 indicated earlier that farmers the world over are always optimists. Perhaps no other segment of society has to deal more closely with the elements. We hope and trust this spirit continues and that other segments of our society and all levels of government will work together to provide the assistance for Canadians so seriously affected by this quirk of Mother Nature's.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, food is the first essential of human life. The magnitude of the problems can affect each and every Canadian if these conditions continue. I urge the co-operation of all parties and the ministers involved in working toward the successful implementation of the programs outlined by the government today in the interests of all Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first let me state my appreciation to the ten hon. members opposite who have waited so patiently and cut short their weekends so that they might sit under the influence of my spellbinding oratory.
I am pleased to have an opportunity to bring a somewhat different perspective to the matter of water supply in western Canada. 1 was pleased to hear the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) make reference to crop insurance and, inasmuch as we have somme officials of the Department of Agriculture in our midst, I would like to note that I am a great advocate of the
Agricultural Drought
crop insurance program. It has been of tremendous value to Canadian farmers coast to coast. 1 know it inside and out. 1 was employed by the B.C. ministry of agriculture in the crop insurance branch for more than ten years prior to coming to play this role. I do not know of another country in the world which has a better program. Few, if any, can match its effectiness. Certainly the insurance program offered south of the border cannot compare. Crop insurance effectively minimizes the effect of partial losses which farmers suffer from causes beyond their control, mainly weather-produced losses such as the drought circumstance which we are discussing today.
However, crop insurance does not always capably cope with those disastrous situations in which total crop losses are experienced, and this is particularly true of the tree fruit industry where expenses continue whether crops materialize or are lost. We must be prepared to strengthen the ability of that worthy program to protect against those most damaging losses which are presently in some circumstances subject to unsatisfactory limitations.
Not only do we have a water drought in the west; we also have a Liberal drought, and we have a Liberal government policy drought which ignores important economic and social factors of western aspirations.

speechtext:
I thank my friend. Agriculture is possible in the southern interior of B.C. only because the pioneers of that area-my father included-saw the possibilities and took the opportunities presented to them. As a result, the first efforts of these pioneer developers were to produce facilities such as
dams, weirs and diversions to store and to husband that most precious commodity on which our civilization hangs. Thus we find originally a system of earth dams with distribution of water by open ditches, completed at minimal cost with human and horse powered effort, often on a volunteer basis-the human part, I mean. Effective in their day, these simple works have been gradually superseded by increasingly more complex and constly systems adapting to the technology which became available, as science and ingenuity brought us advantage and efficiencies in construction and equipment.
In my remarks to the House on May 16 respecting the farm improvement loans bill 1 made mention of some of the government initiatives which have been of particular value to agriculture in British Columbia. One of those initiatives which has transformed the face of the southern interior of B.C. has been the joint federal-provincial program commonly called ARDA. Without the assistance available from the ARDA program, my own community of Kaleden would be totally different both in appearance and in optimistic outlook, and so too would most of the southern interior of B.C. 1 well recall days in my youth when water was in short summer supply because of limited winter snowpack in the surrounding hills which provided a too short period of runoff. I recollect water rationing measures which affected fruit production and farmers' incomes from the orchards of that area. So I speak on this subject with considerable empathy with those agriculturists now suffering in the drought areas of our nation.
We must accept our role as representatives of the people and do everything possible to bring relief to those so affected. We cannot, of course, legislate rain, and therefore 1 have listened attentively to the speeches presented in this House and in committee by those most familiar with the problems attendant with the drought in the specific areas they represent. Their deep concern is evidenced in the calibre of proposals which they have set before the House.
I trust that hon. members opposite will not be too proud to give adequate attention to the specific suggestions put forward by hon. members on this side whose ridings, constituents, friends and families are in the drought areas and whose concerns reflect a deep awareness of the implications which the drought carries, implications which require an attentive reaction totally free of political strategies.
Let me say something about my own area, something which, at first sight, seems to be a contradiction. The Okanagan-Similkameen area is renowned for the production of tree fruits of incomparable excellence, quality and appearance. This area is now attaining an equal reputation for super grape production, with most of that production destined for the grape crushers of Canada's newest and finest wineries. We have market gardens, ground crops and cattle farms. These verdant agricultural endeavours blossom and flourish in a desert. The natural vegetation on much of the land is bunch grass, sage bush and greasewood.

In speaking to the motion and the release put out by prairie members of Parliament in regard to the drastic drought condition, we have stated a number of options we would like to see the Liberal government follow. One such option is that the Department of Finance should bring in income averaging. The hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenbcrger) on a number of occasions brought this proposal before the Eiouse of Commons. 1 should like to refer his speech of on February 26, 1979, in which he referred to a study that was done by Peat Marwick and Partners for the Alberta department of agriculture entitled "Feasibility of an Income Averaging Trust Account". The objective of this plan was that farmers would deposit a portion of their income during high revenue and withdraw funds in lower income years. This would give the farming population faced with such conditions as the current one an opportunity to equalize their incomes.
During the short period of time that my party was in government, we brought forward a number of positive proposals as they pertain to the agricultural sector in Canada. We laid them before the House of Commons, or were in the process of laying them before the House of Commons. Even though they do not affect directly the drought situation as it exits in western Canada, they affect the agricultural sector throughout Canada.
I wish to review some of those positive proposals. The reason I do so is to compare them with the action, or I should say inaction of the present Liberal administration regarding the very serious drought situation as it exists especially in Saskatchewan. In our budget which the other parties saw fit to defeat, we included significant capital gains relief for the farming sector. We promised that during the election campaign, and we delivered on that commitment when we were the government. We promised to make the salaries paid to spouses of farmers deductible for income tax purposes. 1 was encouraged to see in the so-called mini-budget brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) that he included such a provision in his economic statement.
Also we promised a meat import law. The hon. member for Medicine Hat had been working on that when he was parliamentary secretary to the minister of agriculture. He had it ready for presentation to the House of Commons. It is my understanding, at least from the commitments we have to date from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), that he is thinking of introducing a meat import law of his own. It remains to be seen whether he will do it or not, because this has been promised in the past.
We came forward with positive proposals. In regard to the drought situation, the hon. member for Medicine Hat who has spoken on this on several occasions in the House of Commons again has come forward with a plan of action which we would
Agricultural Drought
like to see the government adopt. When we read some press stories about what the government will do in regard to the drought situation, it is obvious their concern is only with the appearance of it rather than with exactly what they will do. 1 should like to quote from the Regina Leader-Post of May 27, 1980, the article entitled "Cabinet told to look good even if it can't really help", which reads as follows:
Draft proposals prepared for the federal cabinet on the drought in western Canada have warned that even if the federal government cannot do much to alleviate the impact of the drought, it must appear to be responding to the situation.
We do believe that is good enough. We would like to see some positive action as was outlined by my colleagues who spoke before me. I am referring to positive action not only in regard to the drought situation, but also in regard to the difficulties western agriculture is facing in totality. If the example we were given yesterday in question period by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) is the type of action that the government is taking, obviously once again the western Canadian farmer will be left wanting.

speechtext:
We would like to see Swift Current put on the map, but not through such terrible headlines.
The hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) suggested that the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) wanted to reduce the breeding herds. This is not correct. What he was suggesting was absolutely the opposite, that is, to protect the breeding herds through our taxing system with an income averaging trust account so that cattlemen could run their own stabilization plan. This is something we have called for many times over the last few vears.
It is the cyclical weather swings, among other things, that give rise to the ups and downs of our agricultural income, that make us look first to our provincial and municipal governments for immediate assistance. As a result of this it makes us in western Canada particularly jealous of our natural resources. We see them as the only possibility of making our provinces financially strong enough to ride out the inevitable downswings and catastrophes that face agriculture, Saskatchewan's basic industry.
Yesterday the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) stated that he got 1.3 per cent of the federal budget, and appealed for help in having it increased. 1 should like to take this opportunity to say a few words about the importance of agriculture,

May 30, 1980
Agricultural Drought
not only to our nation but to the world, and about why it is so important to keep it viable, giving producers confidence to face the futre, most especially the young people who will be entering agriculture.
Our good friends to the south are way ahead of us in the way they are placing great stress on scientific agriculture. Agricultural colleges in the United States are now filled with the brightest young students. There is some excitement about agriculture down there which we do not have in Canada. I am sure the Americans have made the decision, looking ahead, that as they run down their natural resources, high technology and their ability to produce food will be the two great strengths of that nation.
I would like to look ahead one generation to the year 2000. The trouble with looking ahead is, of course, that it seems to be so distant and so far away; we can hardly imagine it. However, if we look back one generation, 1960 is the same distance back as the year 2000 is ahead, but it only seems like yesterday. What did we have one generation ago? We had gold selling for $37 an ounce and wheat selling to the Russians and Chinese at $2.60 per bushel. Now gold is $500 an ounce and wheat is selling at about $6 a bushel. As one of my colleagues said sometime ago, during the last generation we enjoyed cheap energy, cheap money, and cheap food. Now as we enter the eighties we see that cheap energy has gone, cheap money has gone, and 1 suspect that the era of cheap food will be the next to go. Two of the three have already gone.
Let us take a look at the importance of agriculture to Canada and the world in the area of security and co-operation. Surely it was agricultural deeds, the ability to produce food and move it commercially around the world, that opened up the links between the eastern and western worlds. I can think of the exchanges that followed, technical, economic and cultural, and I am sure this has been the greatest influence on security and co-operation that our world has seen in the last 20 years.
If we look ahead one generation the experts say world population will be up by 50 per cent. That means there will be six billion souls in the world. Arable land will decrease by 25 million acres, and for the first time agriculture will not be devoting its resources to producing food, but more and more to producing fuel. We will find food production competing with energy, with all the inputs required. This year alone Brazil will be planting more acres to sugar cane for alcohol production than the total world planting of sugar cane five years ago. We also must give some thought to the moral implications of this food versus fuel situation.
At the very local level, much as I admire PFRA, they seem more concerned right now in southwestern Saskatchewan about moving some cottage owners off a small dam, Duncairn Dam, than they are in working toward a solution of our water problems. As a first step I suggest once again that the minister give consideration to putting PFRA back into agriculture where it belongs.
In the southwest corner of Saskatchewan we have a tremendous aquifer. So far there is only one well drilled down to it.
This requires drilling about 1,400 feet and is very expensive, $40,000 a well. We have only one. Surely some work could be done on this resource.
The hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchinski) spoke about the farmer taking a chance, going ahead and seeding in spite of high interest, lack of moisture and low prices for his products. I think this attitude of farmers can be summed up in the one word "craft", which to me is a combination of skill and cunning. It is something that no government will ever really understand.
It is my understanding that the flood damage compensation from last year's Manitoba floods has still not been paid out. Surely we must have faster action than that. Compensation should now be in the process of being paid out for the flood of people to Winnipeg and other cities as a result of the move from the forest fire regions. There should be federal contribution to forest fire labour expenditures, and it should be immediate. Once again, immediate steps should be taken to protect our breeding herds for the livestock industry. We must have some long-range planning to protect our most important industry in Canada, agriculture, for its contribution to our nation's well being and to others will be one of our greatest assets in the years to come. 1 urge the minister to do everything he can to expedite some fast action in this regard.
