speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) wanted to say a few words, but I will be very brief. 1 will take just a few moments to indicate my concern as well about the drought situation on the prairies, and the concern that has been expressed to me by a number of people in the last few weeks.
I concur in what other western members are saying, and that is that the federal government must act as quickly as possible, and must do all that is possible to alleviate the situation facing our people.
The hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Hamilton) pointed out the importance of food and agriculture in our economy and in the world. I want to concur with that, and to say that if we have to budget a few extra dollars now to help compensate farmers for the losses they are sustaining, by deferring payments on Farm Credit Corporation loans and the like, then that is a worth-while investment, because these farmers will need that money to maintain their operations, and the production of food is the most important thing that human beings can accomplish. We have a lot of people in this world, and if we do not produce food there will be more and more starvation.
I do not think most members of this House realize that Canada, according to the federal Department of Agriculture, is a net importer of food already, to the tune of $2 billion. If we include oilseeds and grains, according to the Science Council of Canada, by the year 2000 we will still be a net importer of food. This is a fact about a country with a small population, with a skilled work force, and with all the scientific and technical knowledge at our disposal. Still we will not be able to
May 30, 1980

feed ourselves. It is important when we get into a crisis like this that we are willing to invest a few extra bucks to make sure the farmers stay on the land, that they do not sustain losses, that they are helped in the national cause and in the national interest. I believe that to be a very, very important thing, indeed.
Many things can be done in the immediate sense and I have already mentioned a moratorium on loans. I mentioned assistance to get feed out to the prairies for livestock-the federal government could provide money for that-and assistance to farmers to find more water through dug-outs and wells and things of that nature. These are all very important. This is a real crisis, and that must be emphasized as vigorously as possible.
The hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) mentioned how very unfortunate it is that the people who drafted the cabinet memo said that even if the government could not do much, it must appear to be responding to the situation for political reasons. That made a headline on the front page of the Leader-Post-"Cabinet Told to Look Good even if it Cannot really Help". Maybe the advisers got careless when writing to memo. Maybe it should not be leaked, but I do not think memos of that sort should even be written. They just increase the feeling of alienation and cynicism in the country that once again it is "they" in Ottawa who are trying to do a snow job, that they are up to their old trickery and up to no good once again. It just reinforces that kind of feeling. I hope the government will learn from his experience. Even if Ministers feel that way they should not put it in writing. I hope that they do not feel they have to do things for the sake of appearance and just put on all the cosmetics in order to look better. I think the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) can look well if he puts him mind into gear, without all the cosmetics.
These are the things that I am concerned about, that we do what we can to protect the agricultural industry. Farming is our No. 1 industry. It produces a lot of jobs in itself, and also in food processing and transportation. There is also the problem of feeding the world's people.
We have a lot of problems in the west that make farmers very angry and upset. One is the question of the grain boycott. Just the other day the hon. member for Prince Albert pointed out that despite the fact there is a boycott on grain in the world, the Russians are purchasing as much grain now as they did before the boycott. That makes our people very angry. The Argentinians, for example, have tripled their sales of grain to the Soviet Union. Spain is shipping some of its grain to the Soviet Union and buying cheaper grain from the United States where the market is depressed, thus making a profit on the grain they have in storage.
Some companies are shipping grain mysteriously to the Soviet Union. Once ships get out to the centre of the ocean they mysteriously change direction and their cargoes end up in Poland, Romania, and other countries. The Soviet Union ends up buying as much grain as it did before the Carter boycott,
Agricultural Drought
although perhaps at a higher price. The price of grain in Canada and the United States has gone down and the farmer suffers.
Just today the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn) asked questions about lay-offs in the farm machinery industry involving 5,000 workers. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) replied that people are buying fewer tractors, combines and farm machinery. This is because their income is not as good. The grain boycott affects them, the drought will affect them, and high interest rates affect them. All these things add up, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT RESPONSE REGARDING AGRICULTURAL DROUGHT AND FOREST FIRE EMERGENCY
speechtext: We had a record export this year.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT RESPONSE REGARDING AGRICULTURAL DROUGHT AND FOREST FIRE EMERGENCY
speechtext:
Yes, we have good exports but the price has fallen. When the cost of production goes up and the price falls, even though the exports increase it does not mean the net income of the farmer increases. The farmer is caught in a cost-price squeeze and that is one of the reasons he is buying less farm machinery. The consequence is lay-offs in Brantford and other farm machinery plants in Canada and North America. The only way of putting those workers back to work is to improve the farm economy.
These are several of the problems we face on the prairies. I am not going into them in detail. One way to alleviate them is to try to get extra money from Treasury Board to be spent on helping farmers in need through moratoriums on loans, helping them find more water supplies, feed supplies for cattle to make sure that the basic herds are not sold off and that some marginal farmers are not forced off the land. All this may cost a little more in the short run, Mr. Speaker. 1 suggest it would be a good investment in the long run, however, to protect the farmers and people of this country, our No. 1 industry and the most important commodity in the world, food.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT RESPONSE REGARDING AGRICULTURAL DROUGHT AND FOREST FIRE EMERGENCY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT RESPONSE REGARDING AGRICULTURAL DROUGHT AND FOREST FIRE EMERGENCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take great pleasure in participating in this debate which has been an excellent one. There have been good speeches and excellent contributions by members from all sides of the House. 1 should like to commend the government on its conciliatory approach to this very urgent and pressing problem. It is a very serious problem and one for which the government must take a great deal of responsibility. Clearly the federal and the provincial governments of the day have a heavy responsibility to ensure that the viability of our basic industry, agriculture, is preserved. There were excellent presentations by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave), the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Hamilton) and the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchinski).
It is quite clear that the most pressing problem at the moment is that of the cattle industry. You have been in this House a number of years, Mr. Speaker, and you have heard of the various problems associated with the cattle industry as a result of depressed prices and situations such as the present drought. One wonders just how many blows this important industry can survive. It has undergone a number of setbacks.

May 30, 1980
Agricultural Drought
The fact that the cattle producers of this country are very resilient and enterprising is a tribute to them and the fact that they have been able to survive.
The government must respond with some action. The comments of spokesmen on the government side lead us to expect some positive and affirmative action. The proof of the pudding will be the programs and steps they initiate to deal with this very important problem.
A number of very good speeches have dealt with the importance of the agricultural industry. What is disturbing, however, is that some of the things that have happened in the few months since this government took office show that there has been a plan for the reduction of the initial price of wheat. Wheat is still one of the major commodities produced in western Canada, and this government has seen fit to reduce the initial price effective August 1.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT RESPONSE REGARDING AGRICULTURAL DROUGHT AND FOREST FIRE EMERGENCY
speechtext: Compared to the adjusted price.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT RESPONSE REGARDING AGRICULTURAL DROUGHT AND FOREST FIRE EMERGENCY
speechtext:
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) is saying compared to the initial price set last year. That is true, but the Conservative government that was in power adjusted those prices and paid an interim payment. What in effect has occurred is a reduction in the initial price of some 50 cents per bushel. The minister cannot deny that.
We also have a situation where for a long time-

speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT RESPONSE REGARDING AGRICULTURAL DROUGHT AND FOREST FIRE EMERGENCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Transport had his opportunity to make a speech. I am sorry I missed it, as I do not know whether he covered this point. If he wants to make another speech I am sure the House would concur. 1 would certainly like him to clarify that point. For the life of me 1 cannot understand how a government can reduce an initial price and then suggest it has increased it. The initial price, as it now stands, will be reduced effective August 1. There is no question about that.
I want to turn now to the two-price system. For a long time it has been recognized that the impact of the two-price system has placed a heavy burden on the producer. The current price of wheat for domestic human consumption is between $4 and $5, while the international markets are considerably above that. They were as high as $6.
In terms of looking at it from the point of view of the cost of production of grain, since 1973 when the two-price system was put into effect, there has been an increase of 105.5 per cent. If you take that back to the price established at that time, you would come up with the figure of $6 per bushel. As a government, we were prepared to increase the price. As a matter of fact we had cabinet approval to increase the price of wheat for domestic human consumption to a level of $6 per bushel. That price would have been in effect right now had our government not been defeated. Because of our government's defeat and the
subsequent taking over of the government by the Liberals, the farmers have lost something in the order of $25 million.
We have to address these matters in a very serious way. What is of deep concern to me, and I am sure to many other members of this House, is the fact that this country, even though it has a tremendous agricultural potential, is relying more and more upon imported foods to feed Canadians. In 1978, Canadians spent some $3.25 billion on imported food. That is almost equal to the $3.8 billion that we paid for imported oil products in that particular year.
We have a tremendous potential in Canada for production of food. However, if we were to take away the exports of our grain and oil seeds, we would be very, very heavily reliant upon imports of food and we would have a very negative imbalance in terms of our agricultural trade picture. Notwithstanding the fact that we are able to penetrate the world markets for wheat and oil seeds, and notwithstanding the fact that we are competing against countries that subsidize their producers very heavily-in this connection 1 am thinking of the United States and the European Common Market-we do quite well in feed grains, cereal grains and oil seeds, but there are a number of areas where we do not do as well.
By way of illlustration, in little over a decade our self-sufficiency in peaches has fallen from 40 per cent to 19 per cent; apricots have fallen from 48 to 25 per cent, and tomatoes from 74 to 43 per cent. In 1978, Canada imported $331 million in meats, primarily beef and pork, most of which could be grown and processed in this country. Next 1 come to the potato growers in Canada. Our tariff duty of 37.5 cents per hundredweight is one-half of the U.S. duty on its potato imports.
What we have to do is recognize the potential in terms of the food production in these areas. We hear it said often that Canada does not have an energy shortage. We may have a shortage of oil, but we do not have an energy shortage. We have many alternative forms of energy which we could use for the encouragement and the expansion of market gardening. Great reliance on hot house production, as far as I am concerned, is essential. Surely with the energy potential that we have, we should be co-ordinating that potential with the potential that we have in agriculture so that we can become more self-reliant in the total area of food production.
Clearly, that is one of the challenges of this government and one of the challenges of this House of Commons. More and more of our acreage should be shifted to fruit and vegetable growing. There is much land in this country that is not being used in its most productive way. It means that we have to be a little more enterprising and more innovative. A country that has the potential of feeding itself is on a drift which I believe will be very serious.
Let us go back to the time of the oil crisis. Prior to 1973 it was suggested that we had all kinds of oil. Yes, the reserves were there. The potential was there. But our will and desire to produce and exploit that were not there. We find that condition exists today, particularly in the absence of any definitive policy by this government to develop an energy plan which would provide self-sufficiency for oil in this country.
May 30, 1980

We have heard some very good suggestions today. We have had suggestions with respect to taxation policy which would help to alleviate the burdens and pressures caused by drought situations, such as this. The annual income averaging program, which has been referred, to is a very excellent example. The matter of capital gains is another one. There are a number of these things which form part and parcel of this party's and our government's agricultural policy. Some of those items were defeated in the budget that we presented to this House in December. Now I find it very strange that some of my hon. friends to the left are harping and chastising the Liberal government for its failure to act in a number of these areas.
This party which formed the government in May, 1979, really identified with a number of the agricultural problems in this country. We addressed those problems. We had a plan of action. We brought forth programs. I find it very strange that the NDP, notwithstanding the fact that these programs were for the benefit, particularly of western Canadians and western agricultural industries, did not support those programs. For reasons of political expediency it defeated the budget which was going to transform many of those thoughts and policies into action. In the short period of time that we were a government we did create an improved climate of confidence with respect to grain production in this country, and particularly our ability to move grain to export markets.
I am pleased that my hon. friend, the Minister of 3 ransport, has continued with a number of those programs. 1 have the assurance of the minister personally, and he has given that assurance in the House, that that will continue. I commend him for that stand. If we are going to develop and continue to exploit our export market potential, we must demonstrate to those customers that we have the facility and the capacity to move our grains to an export position when needed.
We have lost many markets. As a matter of fact over $1 billion has been lost in the last two years as a result of our failure and inability to move grain to an export position when our customers demanded it. It is important for the producers
Business of the House
to know that we will have the ability to move that grain to an export position. It is important for them to plan.
I urge this government to deal with this matter very seriously. This drought situation is one of those areas in which it can now act to ensure a continued climate of confidence and stability so that our producers can plan not only for this crop year but for future crop years.
As hon. members know, the amount of foreign exchange generated out of the export of grain and oil seeds to the export market is a very important component of our total economy.
Today we have heard of the impact that any reduction in agricultural revenue and activity has upon the industries of eastern Canada.
1 conclude by saying that this has been an excellent debate. 1 am pleased by the conciliatory attitude of the government. I simply want to say this that that conciliatory attitude will have to be backed up and demonstrated with positive actions and programs to ensure that this agricultural industry, so important to us, can continue to grow, develop, and survive as a vital industry.
Mir. Knowles: Mr. Speaker, may I ask if it is still the intention to return to the debate on Bill C-30 on Monday?

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the government House leader, I can inform the House that that is the intention of the government for Monday, namely, continuing debate on Bill C-30, the Supplementary Borrowing Authority Act.
